sections.title: Security Architecture: Filters, Authentication and Password Storage

blocks.text:
### Password Storage

Every request that reaches a Spring Boot web application passes through the servlet filter chain of the container before any controller is invoked. Spring Security is implemented entirely on that mechanism: a single servlet filter is registered with the container, and that filter hosts an ordered list of security filters that are private to Spring Security. Understanding this arrangement is the prerequisite for every later topic in this part. A misplaced custom filter, a lost authentication in an asynchronous task, a 403 that should have been a 401, and a CORS preflight that fails before the application is consulted are all consequences of the same few classes.

This chapter follows a request from the servlet container to the point where an `Authentication` is stored, describes how credentials are verified by `ProviderManager`, `DaoAuthenticationProvider`, `UserDetailsService` and `PasswordEncoder`, and treats password storage in detail because it is the control whose failure causes the most damage after a data leak. The target versions are Spring Boot 3.4 and 3.5 with Spring Security 6.4 and 6.5 on JDK 21; behaviour that differs from Spring Security 5 is stated explicitly.

### Concept and mechanism

#### From the servlet container to the security filter chain

The servlet container knows nothing about Spring beans. It only accepts `jakarta.servlet.Filter` instances registered through its own API. Spring Security therefore registers one filter, `DelegatingFilterProxy`, under the name `springSecurityFilterChain`. In a Spring Boot application the registration is performed by `SecurityFilterAutoConfiguration` through a `DelegatingFilterProxyRegistrationBean`. At request time `DelegatingFilterProxy` looks up the bean of that name in the `ApplicationContext` (lazily, so that the container can register the filter before the context exists) and delegates `doFilter` to it.

The bean is a `FilterChainProxy`. It holds a `List<SecurityFilterChain>` and, for each request, asks every chain in order whether it matches (`SecurityFilterChain.matches(HttpServletRequest)`). The first matching chain supplies the list of filters; later chains are not consulted. The selected filters are executed by an inner `VirtualFilterChain`, which keeps an index and calls the next filter each time a filter invokes `chain.doFilter`. When the index passes the last filter, control returns to the original container chain and the request proceeds to the `DispatcherServlet`. A filter that does not call `chain.doFilter` ends the request there, which is exactly how authentication failures, CSRF rejections and authorisation denials stop a request before any controller code runs.

`FilterChainProxy` also performs two duties that are independent of the chains. It applies an `HttpFirewall` (`StrictHttpFirewall` by default), which rejects requests with suspicious path content such as encoded slashes, semicolons or percent-encoded periods with an exception, and it clears the `SecurityContextHolder` in a `finally` block so that no authentication leaks to the next request served by the same thread.

blocks.text:
In application code a chain is declared as a `SecurityFilterChain` bean built from `HttpSecurity`. Each `@Bean` produces one `DefaultSecurityFilterChain`, consisting of a `RequestMatcher` (set with `securityMatcher`, or "any request" when absent) and the filters that the `HttpSecurity` DSL configured. Because the first match wins, a chain without a `securityMatcher` must be ordered last with `@Order`. An any-request chain ordered before another chain fails at startup, because the later chain could never be invoked.

#### The default filters and their order

The order of the filters is not defined by the order of the DSL calls. `HttpSecurity` sorts filters with a `FilterOrderRegistration` that assigns each known filter class a fixed position. This is why `addFilterBefore(f,` `X.class)` and `addFilterAfter(f, X.class)` take a reference class: the custom filter receives the position of the reference class, offset by one. A typical servlet application with form login and HTTP Basic produces the following list at startup (logged at DEBUG by `DefaultSecurityFilterChain` with the prefix `Will secure any request with`; the Spring Security reference shows the same sequence).

blocks.text: The responsibilities of the filters that matter for most diagnoses are the following.

rows: Loads the `SecurityContext` from the `SecurityContextRepository` (the HTTP session by default) into a deferred supplier; since Spring Security 6 it never saves it implicitly
Answers CORS preflights and adds CORS headers; present only if `cors(...)` is configured
Rejects unsafe methods without a valid token with 403
Processes `POST /login`; builds an unauthenticated token and calls the `AuthenticationManager`
Extracts `Authorization: Bearer`, authenticates through `JwtAuthenticationProvider`; present with `oauth2ResourceServer`
Places an `AnonymousAuthenticationToken` when no authentication exists
Catches `AuthenticationException` and `AccessDeniedException` and converts them into 401 or 403 responses
Evaluates the `authorizeHttpRequests` rules; the last decision point before the servlet
blocks.caption: Filters that determine most observable behaviour.

blocks.text:
Two changes from Spring Security 5 explain frequent migration defects. First, `SecurityContextPersistenceFilter` was replaced by `SecurityContextHolderFilter`, and the authentication filters now save the context themselves; a custom filter that sets `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(...)` on a request that is later followed by a second request in the same session must also call `SecurityContextRepository.saveContext(...)` if the authentication is meant to survive in the session. For a stateless API this is irrelevant, because the authentication is rebuilt from the token on each request. Second, `FilterSecurityInterceptor` was replaced by `AuthorizationFilter`, which authorises every dispatch type (`REQUEST`, `ERROR`, `FORWARD`, `ASYNC`) unless configured otherwise; the reference documentation recommends permitting `FORWARD` and `ERROR` dispatches explicitly when error pages are used.

The mechanism is small enough to reproduce with plain Java. The following program implements the same structure: an index-based chain, filters that either continue or end the request, and a thread-local context holder. It then repeats the run with the authentication filter placed after the authorisation filter, which is the most common mistake with custom filters.

blocks.title: MiniSecurity.java

blocks.code:
$ java MiniSecurity.java
Correct order:  /orders headers={Authorization=Bearer good}
   > SecurityContextHolderFilter
   > BearerTokenFilter (authentication)
   > AuthorizationFilter
   => controller runs, user=alice
   < AuthorizationFilter
   < BearerTokenFilter (authentication)
   < SecurityContextHolderFilter

Wrong order (custom filter after AuthorizationFilter):  /orders headers={Authorization=Bearer good}
   > SecurityContextHolderFilter
   > AuthorizationFilter
   ! no Authentication in context -> denied (anonymous): 401
   < AuthorizationFilter
   < SecurityContextHolderFilter

request thread sees user=alice
worker thread sees user=null
blocks.title: Mini filter chain: correct order, wrong order, thread-local context

blocks.text:
In the second run the request carries a valid token, yet it is rejected, because `AuthorizationFilter` evaluates an empty context. The simplified model signals the failure by returning; real Spring Security throws `AccessDeniedException`, which `ExceptionTranslationFilter` converts into a 401 for an anonymous caller and a 403 for an authenticated one. The last two lines show that a different thread does not see the authentication, a property examined below.

#### Authentication objects and the authentication manager

`Authentication` is the central data type. It exposes `getPrincipal()` (the user, usually a `UserDetails` or a `Jwt`), `getCredentials()` (the password or token before verification, cleared afterwards), `getAuthorities()` (a collection of `GrantedAuthority`) and `isAuthenticated()`. Authentication code does not construct this interface directly; it uses `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(principal, credentials)` before verification and `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.authenticated(principal, credentials, authorities)` after it. The factory methods exist since Spring Security 5.7 and replace constructors whose boolean state was implicit.

The verification contract is `AuthenticationManager.authenticate(Authentication)`, which returns a fully populated `Authentication` or throws an `AuthenticationException`. The standard implementation, `ProviderManager`, holds a list of `AuthenticationProvider` instances. For each provider it calls `supports(Class<?>)` and, when the provider accepts the token type, `authenticate`. A provider that returns `null` abstains; a provider that throws `AccountStatusException` stops the iteration, while other `AuthenticationException` values are remembered and the next provider is tried. If no provider succeeds and a parent `AuthenticationManager` is configured, the parent is consulted. This arrangement explains why one application can accept form logins, API keys and JWTs side by side: each mechanism contributes its own provider or its own chain.

For username and password the provider is `DaoAuthenticationProvider`, which extends `AbstractUserDetailsAuthenticationProvider`. Its work is deterministic:

1. Load the `UserDetails` through `UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername`.
2. Run the pre-authentication checks (`UserDetailsChecker`): account not locked, enabled, not expired.
3. Compare the submitted password with the stored hash using `PasswordEncoder.matches`.
4. Run the post-authentication check on credential expiry.
5. If `PasswordEncoder.upgradeEncoding` reports that the hash is outdated and a `UserDetailsPasswordService` bean exists, re-encode the raw password and store the new hash.
6. Build the authenticated token and, because `ProviderManager` has `eraseCredentialsAfterAuthentication` enabled by default, remove the credentials from it.

By default `hideUserNotFoundExceptions` is true: an unknown user name produces the same `BadCredentialsException` as a wrong password, and the provider hashes a dummy password for unknown users so that the response time does not reveal whether an account exists. A custom `UserDetailsService` that throws other exception types or returns early can defeat this protection.

blocks.text:
When Spring Boot finds exactly one `UserDetailsService` bean (and a `PasswordEncoder`), it builds the default `AuthenticationManager` from them; the generated in-memory user and its logged password (`Using generated` `security password`) appear only when no such bean exists. Exposing the `AuthenticationManager` as a bean, needed for a JSON login endpoint, is done with `AuthenticationConfiguration.getAuthenticationManager()` and is shown in the chapter on JWT.

#### The SecurityContextHolder and threads

`SecurityContextHolder` stores the `SecurityContext` (a holder of one `Authentication`) through a `SecurityContextHolderStrategy`. The default, `MODE_THREADLOCAL`, binds the context to the current thread. This matches the thread-per-request model of Tomcat: the filter chain and the controller run on one thread, so any code can read the current user without parameters. The consequence is that code running on a different thread, such as an `@Async` method, a `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` task or an executor submission, does not see the authentication. `MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL` copies the context when a thread is created, which is unreliable with pooled threads because a pooled thread keeps the context of the request that created it. `MODE_GLOBAL` shares one context for the whole JVM and is appropriate only for single-user desktop clients. The mode is selected with the system property `spring.security.strategy` or `SecurityContextHolder.setStrategyName`.

The supported solution is to wrap the executor so that the context is captured when a task is submitted and installed on the worker thread for the duration of the task. `DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor` and `DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor` do this. Since Spring Security 5.8 the preferred way to access the holder inside components is to inject a `SecurityContextHolderStrategy` bean rather than calling the static methods, which keeps the behaviour testable. Virtual threads (`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`, Spring Boot 3.2 and later) do not change the rule: each virtual thread has its own thread-local values, so the same propagation is required.

### Password storage

A password database must be assumed to leak eventually. The purpose of password hashing is to make the leaked data as expensive as possible to turn into passwords. Three properties are required of the stored value. It must be derived by a one-way function, so that the password cannot be computed from the hash. It must include a per-user random salt, so that equal passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless. It must be deliberately slow, and for modern functions also memory-hungry, so that each guess costs an attacker real resources. General-purpose digests such as SHA-256 satisfy only the first property and are designed to be fast, which is the opposite of the third requirement.

The effect of the cost parameter is directly measurable with the JDK, which contains PBKDF2 (`PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256`). The following program times the function for increasing iteration counts, demonstrates the salt property, uses the constant-time comparison `MessageDigest.isEqual`, and compares the guess rate against a single SHA-256 call.

The reference documentation advises tuning the work factor so that one verification takes about one second on production hardware where the login rate permits it. Many applications choose a smaller value, typically 100 to 300 ms, because every login consumes a request thread for that time; this trade-off is itself a denial-of-service consideration and is the reason for rate limiting login attempts (see the chapter on web attacks and defences). The factory-method defaults named above are version-dependent; the Javadoc of the version in use is authoritative.

#### DelegatingPasswordEncoder and algorithm migration

Hash formats age. A stored value that carries no information about its algorithm cannot be migrated without a flag day. `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` solves this by storing an identifier in braces in front of every hash, for example `{bcrypt}$2a$10$...`. `matches` reads the identifier, selects the encoder registered under it, and delegates. `encode` always uses the configured default identifier. A value without an identifier is handled by a configurable fallback encoder (`setDefaultPasswordEncoderForMatches`); in the default factory this fallback throws `IllegalArgumentException:` `There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id "null"`, a frequent error after a migration from Spring Security 4.

blocks.text: Migration relies on `upgradeEncoding(String)`. `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` returns true when the identifier differs from the current default, and the individual encoders return true when their stored cost is lower than the configured cost. `DaoAuthenticationProvider` evaluates this after a successful password match and, if the application defines a `UserDetailsPasswordService`, calls it with the raw password re-encoded by the current default. Over time every active account moves to the new algorithm without a forced reset. The worked example below implements the service.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How should passwords be stored, and why is SHA-256 with a salt not sufficient? A one-way, salted, deliberately slow and preferably memory-hard function should be used (bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count), selected through `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` so that parameters can be raised later. Salted SHA-256 prevents rainbow tables but evaluates in nanoseconds, so a leaked database falls to GPU guessing at billions of attempts per second; the measurement above shows a factor of about 10^5 between one SHA-256 call and one PBKDF2 verification at 310,000 iterations.

### Worked example

The example is the account layer of an order service. It consists of a JPA entity, a repository, a `UserDetailsService` that also implements `UserDetailsPasswordService`, a security configuration with two chains, and a registration endpoint. The package is `com.example.shop`. Spring Security and Spring Data JPA are on the classpath (`spring-boot-starter-security`, `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`, `spring-boot-starter-web`). The Spring code in this chapter was not run on the build machine, because no Spring artefacts are available there; class and method names were checked against the Spring Security 6.5 reference documentation.

blocks.title: AppUser.java (accessors omitted)
AppUserRepository.java

blocks.text: The `UserDetailsService` maps the entity to Spring Security's `User` builder. Roles are stored without a prefix; the builder method `roles(...)` adds `ROLE_` and rejects values that already carry it, which makes the prefix convention explicit in one place.

blocks.title: JpaUserDetailsService.java

blocks.text: The configuration declares two chains. The first matches only `/api/**`, is stateless and uses HTTP Basic for this chapter; the chapter on JWT replaces Basic with bearer tokens. The second chain serves browser pages with a form login and a server-side session. The password encoder is a `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` with bcrypt at strength 12 as the default for new hashes and the legacy identifiers needed for migration.

blocks.title: SecurityConfig.java

blocks.text: Disabling CSRF in the API chain is justified only because the chain is stateless and authenticates with a header that a browser does not attach automatically; HTTP Basic credentials cached by the browser would reopen the CSRF exposure, which is why the later chapters use bearer tokens. The reasoning is developed in the chapter on web attacks and defences.

blocks.title: RegistrationController.java

blocks.text:
The maximum password length of 128 characters is deliberate. An unbounded field turns the slow hash into a denial-of-service amplifier, because hashing a megabyte-sized password costs far more than the nominal work factor suggests. The minimum of 12 follows current guidance to prefer length over composition rules.

### Hands-on

With `logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG` in `application.properties`, startup prints the filters of each chain, which is the quickest way to verify ordering. The following output is **typical output (not run on the build** **machine)**; the exact filter list depends on the DSL calls and on the starters present.

For a trace of one request, `logging.level.org.springframework.security=TRACE` prints each filter entered (`Invoking` `BasicAuthenticationFilter (6/12)`), the authentication attempt and the authorisation decision. A line stating `Set` `SecurityContextHolder to anonymous SecurityContext` followed by `Failed to authorize ... with attributes` `authenticated` identifies a request that reached `AuthorizationFilter` without credentials.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: a custom authentication filter runs after authorisation

**Scenario.** A team adds an `ApiKeyFilter` as a bean implementing `OncePerRequestFilter` and registers it with `http.addFilterAfter(apiKeyFilter, AuthorizationFilter.class)` because the filter list in an example used that class as the reference.

**Symptoms.** Every request with a valid key receives 401 or 403. A breakpoint in the filter is reached only after the response status has been decided. In some deployments the filter is additionally executed twice.

**Diagnosis.** Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG` and read the `Will secure ...` line: the custom filter appears after `AuthorizationFilter`. At TRACE level the sequence of `Invoking ... Filter` messages confirms that authorisation ran first. The plain-Java model above shows the same effect. The double execution occurs when the filter is also a Spring bean: Spring Boot registers every `Filter` bean with the servlet container as well, so it runs once in the container chain and once in the security chain.

**Root cause.** Authorisation reads the `SecurityContext` that earlier filters must have populated; a filter placed after `AuthorizationFilter` populates it too late. The bean registration is an independent defect.

**Fix.** Place the filter before the filter that would otherwise authenticate, and prevent the container registration.

blocks.title: ApiKeyFilterConfig.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Do not annotate security filters with `@Component`; construct them inside the configuration method. Add a test that asserts the filter position, or a `MockMvc` test with and without the key.

#### Problem 2: passwords stored with an unsalted fast hash

**Scenario.** A legacy table `app_user` holds `password_hash` values that are 64 hexadecimal characters, produced by one SHA-256 call without salt. A penetration test shows that most of the table is recovered within minutes.

**Symptoms.** Rows with equal passwords have equal hashes; a dictionary attack recovers common passwords; every login takes under a millisecond.

**Diagnosis.** Inspect the data and the code: `SELECT password_hash, count(*) FROM app_user GROUP BY 1 HAVING` `count(*) > 1` returns duplicate hashes, which proves the absence of a salt. A grep for `MessageDigest` or `DigestUtils` in the login code identifies the algorithm.

**Root cause.** The function is fast and unsalted, so the cost of each guess is negligible and one computation serves every account with that password.

**Fix.** Mark the legacy values with an identifier and let the delegating encoder migrate users on login. Forced resets are unnecessary for active accounts. The migration needs one SQL statement and one registered legacy encoder.

blocks.title: V12__mark_legacy_hashes.sql
LegacyEncoders.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
After a successful login, `upgradeEncoding` returns true for `{legacy-sha256}` values, and `JpaUserDetailsService.updatePassword` stores a bcrypt hash. Accounts that remain dormant keep the weak hash; a second step wraps them as `bcrypt(sha256hex)` offline or invalidates them after a deadline. Because the stored legacy values were leaked in the incident, sessions and reset tokens should also be rotated.

**Prevention.** Reject any use of `MessageDigest` for passwords in code review, keep the identifier prefix mandatory, and define the target encoder in one configuration class.

#### Problem 3: the authenticated user is unknown inside an asynchronous task

**Scenario.** A controller returns immediately and delegates report generation to an `@Async` service method that records the current user name in an audit table.

**Symptoms.** The audit column contains `null` or the method fails with `AuthenticationCredentialsNotFoundException` when it carries `@PreAuthorize`. The synchronous variant works.

**Diagnosis.** Log `Thread.currentThread().getName()` in both places: the controller runs on `http-nio-8080-exec-N`, the method on `task-N`. Log `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()` in the second thread; it is `null`. The plain-Java output above reproduces this (`worker thread sees user=null`).

**Root cause.** The default `MODE_THREADLOCAL` strategy does not propagate the context to other threads.

**Fix.** Wrap the executor used by `@Async` with `DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor`.

blocks.title: AsyncConfig.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Pass the user identifier as an explicit method argument for work that outlives the request; a background job that runs minutes later should not depend on a request-scoped authentication at all.

#### Problem 4: brute-force login attempts

**Scenario.** The login endpoint receives thousands of attempts per minute from a rotating set of addresses against a small set of user names (credential stuffing).

**Symptoms.** A spike in `401` responses on `/login` or `/api/**`, high CPU on application nodes (each failed attempt still costs a full hash verification), and successful logins of real users from unusual locations.

**Diagnosis.** Count failures per user name and per source address from the access log or from a Micrometer counter incremented in an `AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent` listener. CPU profiles show `BCrypt.hashpw` or `PBEKeySpec` frames at the top.

**Root cause.** The endpoint accepts unlimited attempts, and the slow hash that protects stored passwords makes each attempt expensive for the server as well.

**Fix.** Combine a per-account backoff with a per-source rate limit at the edge. The per-account policy below (run as plain Java) doubles the lock time after each failure beyond five; a lock based only on the user name lets an attacker lock out real users, so it should be paired with the rate limit and with notification.

blocks.text: In Spring the failure counting is attached to authentication events, which `DefaultAuthenticationEventPublisher` publishes without configuration for most failures.

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Rate limit by address and by account, require multi-factor authentication for sensitive roles, check new passwords against breached-password lists, and alert on failure ratios.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is the relationship between** `DelegatingFilterProxy`**,** `FilterChainProxy` **and** `SecurityFilterChain`**?** `DelegatingFilterProxy` is the only filter known to the servlet container and forwards to the bean named `springSecurityFilterChain`, which is a `FilterChainProxy`. That bean selects the first `SecurityFilterChain` whose matcher accepts the request and runs its filters.
2. **Why does the order of security filters matter?** Later filters rely on the results of earlier ones: `AuthorizationFilter` reads the `SecurityContext` that an authentication filter must have populated, and `ExceptionTranslationFilter` must wrap `AuthorizationFilter` to translate its exceptions. `HttpSecurity` sorts filters by a fixed registry, so custom filters are positioned relative to a reference class.
3. **How does** `ProviderManager` **work?** It iterates over its `AuthenticationProvider` list, calling `supports` and then `authenticate`; the first provider that returns a result ends the iteration, and a parent manager is consulted when none succeeds.
4. **Where does the authenticated user live between filters and controllers, and what is the limitation?** In `SecurityContextHolder`, by default a thread-local. Other threads, including `@Async` workers, do not see it unless the executor is wrapped with the delegating security-context classes.
5. **Why is a salt required, and where is it stored?** It makes equal passwords produce different hashes and defeats precomputed tables. It is stored in the hash string itself (for bcrypt the 22 characters after the cost field), so no separate column is needed.
6. **What does** `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` **provide?** An identifier prefix per hash, so that several algorithms coexist and the default can change; together with `upgradeEncoding` it allows migration at login time.
7. **Why does** `DaoAuthenticationProvider` **return the same error for an unknown user and a wrong** **password?** To prevent user enumeration; it also performs a dummy password comparison so that the response times match.
8. **What changed from** `SecurityContextPersistenceFilter` **to** `SecurityContextHolderFilter`**?** The context is loaded lazily and is no longer saved automatically at the end of the request; authentication mechanisms save it explicitly through the `SecurityContextRepository`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A single container filter (`DelegatingFilterProxy`) hosts `FilterChainProxy`, which selects the first matching `SecurityFilterChain` per request; filter order is fixed by a registry, not by declaration order.
- `ProviderManager` delegates to `AuthenticationProvider` instances; `DaoAuthenticationProvider` combines `UserDetailsService` and `PasswordEncoder` and hides whether a user exists.
- The `SecurityContextHolder` is thread-bound by default; asynchronous work needs an executor that copies the context.
- Passwords are stored as salted, slow, memory-hard hashes behind `DelegatingPasswordEncoder`, with `upgradeEncoding` driving migration; measured PBKDF2 at 310,000 iterations cost about 80 ms against

sub-microsecond SHA-256.

- Diagnose with the DEBUG filter list and TRACE logs before changing configuration.

sections.title: Authorisation: Request Rules, Method Security and Ownership

blocks.text:
### Ownership

Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorisation decides what that caller may do. The two are implemented by different filters and fail with different status codes, and most production defects in this area come from confusing them: rules in the wrong order, a role prefix that does not match, a method annotation that is silently ignored, or an endpoint that checks the role but not the owner of the record. This chapter describes the authorisation pipeline for HTTP requests (`AuthorizationFilter` and `AuthorizationManager`), the method-level mechanism built on proxies, and the design of object-level (ownership) checks, which role checks cannot express.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Authorities, roles and prefixes

Spring Security reduces every permission to a `GrantedAuthority`, a wrapper around a string. A role is an authority whose string starts with the prefix `ROLE_`. The distinction is purely a naming convention supported by two families of methods: `hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")` compares the string exactly, while `hasRole("ADMIN")` prepends the prefix first. `hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN")` in the Java DSL is rejected at startup because the prefix is added automatically; inside SpEL expressions the check is more tolerant. The default prefix can be changed with a `GrantedAuthorityDefaults` bean, but doing so affects only the role-based methods and leaves `hasAuthority` unchanged.

Authorities originate in the authentication mechanism. With `UserDetails` they are whatever the `UserDetailsService` returned; with a JWT resource server they are produced by `JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter`, which by default maps the `scope` or `scp` claim to authorities prefixed with `SCOPE_`. A token with `"scope": "orders:read orders:write"` therefore yields `SCOPE_orders:read` and `SCOPE_orders:write`, and `hasRole("ADMIN")` cannot match any of them. Every "authenticated but denied" investigation begins by printing the actual authorities of the `Authentication`.

A `RoleHierarchy` expresses that one role implies others. `RoleHierarchyImpl.fromHierarchy("ROLE_ADMIN >` `ROLE_USER")` (Spring Security 6.3 and later) makes an administrator pass every `hasRole("USER")` check. The hierarchy applies to request rules when the bean is present, and to method security when it is passed to the `MethodSecurityExpressionHandler`, as shown below.

#### URL authorisation with AuthorizationFilter

`AuthorizationFilter` is the last filter of the chain. It obtains an `AuthorizationManager<HttpServletRequest>`, which for the `authorizeHttpRequests` DSL is a `RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager`. This object holds an ordered list of pairs (`RequestMatcher`, `AuthorizationManager<RequestAuthorizationContext>`). For a request, the first pair whose matcher accepts the request decides; later pairs are never consulted. The manager returns an `AuthorizationDecision`; a negative decision causes the filter to throw `AccessDeniedException`.

The `Authentication` is passed as a `Supplier`, so it is read lazily: `permitAll()` and `denyAll()` never touch the session or the token. Built-in managers cover the common cases (`AuthenticatedAuthorizationManager`, `AuthorityAuthorizationManager`), and `AuthorizationManagers.allOf(...)` and `anyOf(...)` combine them. A custom manager is passed to `access(...)` as an object or a lambda.

ExceptionTranslationFilter | AuthenticationEntryPoint anonymous | 401 / redirect to login | authenticated caller? | AccessDeniedHandler | 403 Forbidden not anonymous

blocks.text:
Four properties of the rule list explain most defects.

- **Order is semantics.** A general rule placed before a specific one hides it. The reference documentation recommends ending the list with `anyRequest().denyAll()`, which turns the rules into an allow list.
- **Matching is path-based.** Query parameters and headers do not take part; a custom `RequestMatcher` is required for those.
- **Pattern interpretation.** With Spring MVC on the classpath, `requestMatchers(String...)` produces matchers that agree with MVC path matching. Since Spring Framework 6 a trailing slash no longer matches by default, so a rule for `/orders` does not cover `/orders/`, and the MVC mapping does not either; both then yield 404 rather than a rule bypass, but tests should include the variant. When several servlets are registered (for example the H2 console), the DSL cannot decide which pattern dialect applies and fails at startup with a message asking for an explicit matcher.
- **Dispatch types.** Authorisation also applies to `ERROR` and `FORWARD` dispatches. An application that renders error pages must permit those dispatch types, otherwise the error path itself is denied and the client sees a bare 401 or 403 instead of the intended error response.

The rule evaluation is small enough to model in plain Java. The program below evaluates an ordered rule list, applies a role hierarchy, and reports the status that `ExceptionTranslationFilter` would produce. It reproduces two typical defects: a general rule placed first, and an authority that lacks the `ROLE_` prefix.

blocks.title: RuleMatcher.java

blocks.code:
$ java RuleMatcher.java
-- correct order
anonymous  /admin/users : 401 (entry point)   [first match: /admin/** hasRole(ADMIN)]
USER       /admin/users : 403 (denied handler)   [first match: /admin/** hasRole(ADMIN)]
ADMIN      /admin/users : 200 allowed   [first match: /admin/** hasRole(ADMIN)]
USER       /orders      : 200 allowed   [first match: /** authenticated]
-- /** placed before /admin/**
USER       /admin/users : 200 allowed   [first match: /** authenticated]
-- authority ADMIN (no prefix) against hasRole(ADMIN)
ADMIN      /admin/users : 403 (denied handler)   [first match: /admin/** hasRole(ADMIN)]
blocks.title: Ordered rules, first match wins, 401 versus 403

blocks.text:
#### 401 versus 403

The two status codes answer different questions. **401 Unauthorized** means that the request lacks valid authentication; it should carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming the scheme. **403 Forbidden** means that the caller is known and the action is not permitted. `ExceptionTranslationFilter` decides between them: it catches `AccessDeniedException`; if the current authentication is anonymous (or remember-me), it starts authentication through the `AuthenticationEntryPoint` (401, or a redirect to the login page for browser chains); otherwise it delegates to the `AccessDeniedHandler` (403). An `AuthenticationException` thrown by an authentication filter, such as an invalid token, goes to the entry point directly.

The consequence for API design is that the entry point must match the client type. A browser chain redirects to `/login` with status 302, which is meaningless for a JSON client; an API chain should use `HttpStatusEntryPoint` or `BearerTokenAuthenticationEntryPoint`, which returns 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`. Authentication that succeeded followed by 403 never produces a redirect.

#### Method security

Request rules protect URLs; they cannot protect a service method that is reachable from several controllers, from messaging listeners or from scheduled jobs. Method security attaches authorisation to the method itself. It is activated with `@EnableMethodSecurity` (Spring Security 5.6 and later; it supersedes `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`) and enables `@PreAuthorize`, `@PostAuthorize`, `@PreFilter` and `@PostFilter` by default; `@Secured` and JSR-250 annotations require `securedEnabled = true` and `jsr250Enabled = true`. Spring Boot does not enable it automatically.

The implementation is ordinary Spring AOP. `@EnableMethodSecurity` registers advisors whose interceptors are `AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor` (for `@PreAuthorize`) and `AuthorizationManagerAfterMethodInterceptor` (for `@PostAuthorize`). The expression is evaluated by `PreAuthorizeAuthorizationManager` against a `MethodSecurityExpressionRoot` that offers `hasRole`, `hasAuthority`, `authentication`, `principal`, the method arguments by name (`#id`) and, in `@PostAuthorize`, `returnObject`. A denied call raises `AuthorizationDeniedException`, a subclass of `AccessDeniedException` introduced in Spring Security 6.3.

Because the mechanism is a proxy, three limits apply, all inherited from the AOP chapter of the container part: calls from inside the same object (`this.method()`) bypass the proxy; `private` methods and `final` classes or methods cannot be intercepted by the CGLIB subclass; and a bean created with `new` is not proxied at all. The annotation is silently ignored in each case, which is why a test that asserts the denial is mandatory.

blocks.text:
The interceptors are ordered through `AuthorizationInterceptorsOrder`: `@PreFilter` 100, `@PreAuthorize` 200, `@Secured` 300, JSR-250 400, `@PostAuthorize` 500, `@PostFilter` 600. `TransactionInterceptor` defaults to the lowest precedence, so pre-authorisation runs before the transaction opens, which is desirable, whereas `@PostAuthorize` runs after the transaction has committed. A `@PostAuthorize` on a method that writes data therefore does not roll back the write when the check fails; the reference documentation advises against that combination. Annotations on one method are combined conjunctively, and repeating the same annotation is not supported; boolean operators in one expression serve instead.

#### Ownership and the permission model

A role check answers "may this kind of caller perform this kind of action". Most applications also need "may this caller act on this record". Omitting the second question is the defect class known as insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and is listed by OWASP as broken object-level authorisation, the first item of the API Security Top 10. There are four implementation techniques, ordered by preference.

1. **Query-level scoping.** The repository query includes the owner: `findByIdAndOwner(id, owner)`. A record owned by someone else is simply not found, so the endpoint answers 404 and does not confirm that the identifier exists. This is the strongest option because the data is never loaded.
2. **A bean-based expression.** `@PreAuthorize("@orderAuthz.canCancel(#id, authentication)")` delegates to a Spring bean that may consult the database and the business state. It runs before the method and is testable in isolation.
3. `@PostAuthorize`**.** `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.owner == authentication.name")` checks the loaded object. The record is loaded before the decision, which costs a query and, with a side-effecting method, is unsafe.
4. **A** `PermissionEvaluator`**.** `hasPermission(#id, 'Order', 'read')` routes to a registered evaluator. It is suitable when permissions are stored in a table (access-control lists), and it is heavier than the other options.

Every technique reads the identity from the `Authentication`, never from a request parameter or body field. A body containing `"owner": "bob"` that is bound to the entity allows mass assignment of ownership (see the chapter on web attacks).

### Worked example

The example secures an order API. Rules: product browsing is public; ordering requires the user role; deletion and the `/api/admin` area require the administrator role; the administrator inherits the user role; a user sees and cancels only their own orders. The listings continue the `com.example.shop` package of the previous chapter.

Two details are worth noting. `hasRole("USER")` on `/api/**` admits administrators because of the hierarchy, and the DELETE rule precedes the general rule on purpose. In Spring Security 6.4 and later the interface method for a custom manager is named `authorize` and returns an `AuthorizationResult`; the lambda form above targets the `check` contract documented for 6.5 and stays source-compatible in the 6.x line.

### Hands-on

With users `alice` (role USER), `bob` (role USER) and `root` (role ADMIN), and one order owned by alice, the following calls demonstrate each layer. The output is **typical output (not run on the build machine)**.

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/api/orders/1
401
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u alice:pw localhost:8080/api/orders/1
200
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u bob:pw localhost:8080/api/orders/1
404
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u bob:pw -X POST localhost:8080/api/orders/1/cancel
403
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u alice:pw -X DELETE localhost:8080/api/orders/1
403
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u root:pw -X DELETE localhost:8080/api/orders/1
204
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u alice:pw localhost:8080/api/unknown
403
blocks.title: Authorisation outcomes (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
Bob receives 404 for a read (query-level scoping hides the record) and 403 for a cancel (the expression denies). The inconsistency is a design decision to be made deliberately: hiding existence is preferable for reads of private data, and an explicit 403 is acceptable where the identifier is not secret. The final call returns 403 rather than 404 because `denyAll()` decides before routing. With TRACE logging a denied method call shows `AuthorizationDeniedException:` `Access Denied` raised in `AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor` and handled by `ExceptionTranslationFilter`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 5: 401 and 403 returned in the wrong situations

**Scenario.** A single-page client calls the API with an expired bearer token and receives an HTML login page with status 200 after a redirect; another endpoint answers 403 to requests that carry no credentials at all.

**Symptoms.** `fetch` follows a 302 to `/login` and returns HTML that the JSON parser cannot read. Monitoring shows 403 for anonymous traffic on some paths and 401 on others. **Diagnosis.** Log `ExceptionTranslationFilter` at DEBUG; it prints `Sending ... to authentication entry point` `since access is denied` for anonymous callers. Identify which entry point is configured for the matched chain: the log line `Will secure ... with filters` shows which chain applies, and the entry point of a form-login chain is `LoginUrlAuthenticationEntryPoint`. A 403 for anonymous callers arises when `httpBasic`, `formLogin` and `oauth2ResourceServer` are all absent from the chain, because no entry point is registered and `Http403ForbiddenEntryPoint` is the fallback.

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The API paths are served by a chain configured for browsers, or by a chain without any authentication mechanism.

**Fix.** Give API paths a dedicated chain whose entry point returns 401, and keep the redirect behaviour for page paths.

blocks.code:
http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
    .exceptionHandling(e -> e
        .authenticationEntryPoint(new HttpStatusEntryPoint(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED))
        .accessDeniedHandler((req, res, ex) -> res.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN)))
    .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));   // supplies Bearer entry point
blocks.title: ApiEntryPoint.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Test both codes explicitly for each chain: one request without credentials (expect 401) and one with insufficient authority (expect 403).

#### Problem 6: the role check never matches (prefix and mapping mismatch)

**Scenario.** After switching from a database login to JWT, every endpoint protected by `hasRole("ADMIN")` returns 403, although the token of the administrator contains `"roles": ["ADMIN"]`.

**Symptoms.** 403 for users who should pass; the same rule worked before the change.

**Diagnosis.** Print the authorities: a temporary controller method returns `authentication.getAuthorities()`. The output shows `[SCOPE_openid]` or `[ADMIN]`, but not `ROLE_ADMIN`. The plain-Java output above reproduces the effect: authority `ADMIN` against `hasRole(ADMIN)` is denied.

**Root cause.** `hasRole("ADMIN")` requires the authority `ROLE_ADMIN`. The default `JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter` reads only the `scope` or `scp` claims, and produces `SCOPE_` authorities; the `roles` claim is ignored.

**Fix.** Map the claim explicitly in a `JwtAuthenticationConverter`.

blocks.title: JwtRoleConverter.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Document the authority naming scheme once (roles with prefix, permissions without), and assert in a test that the converter yields the expected authorities for a sample token.

#### Problem 7: method security is not applied

**Scenario.** A method annotated `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` is callable by any authenticated user. The annotation is present, the expression is correct, and no error is reported.

**Symptoms.** The method executes for unauthorised callers; no `AuthorizationDeniedException` appears in any log; unit tests that call the service through the Spring context confirm the bypass for some call paths and not for others.

**Diagnosis.** Work through the possible causes in this order. First, check whether `@EnableMethodSecurity` is present on a configuration class; Boot does not add it. Second, check whether the bean is proxied: `AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean)` or a debugger shows a class named `OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0`. Third, check the call path: a call from another method of the same class is a self-invocation. Fourth, check visibility and modifiers: private, static and final methods are not intercepted. Fifth, check whether the object was created with `new` or a `@Bean` method on a `static` factory executed before the infrastructure was ready. The diagram earlier in this chapter shows the self-invocation path.

**Root cause.** The authorisation is attached to the proxy, not to the method body.

**Fix.** Move the protected method into a separate bean or invoke it through the injected proxy; keep the annotation on public methods of non-final beans.

blocks.title: AdminReportService.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** A security test per protected method (`@WithMockUser(roles = "USER")` expecting `AccessDeniedException`) fails when the interception is missing. A catch-all request rule (`/api/admin/**` with `hasRole`) provides a second layer, since the reference documentation states that unannotated methods are not secured.

#### Problem 8: a user reads another user's data (broken object-level authorisation)

**Scenario.** `GET /api/orders/{id}` requires the user role. An authenticated customer iterates identifiers 1, 2, 3 and receives the orders of other customers.

**Symptoms.** Access logs show a single user requesting hundreds of sequential identifiers with status 200; there are no 401 or 403 responses to alert on.

**Diagnosis.** Review the endpoint: the controller calls `repository.findById(id)` without referring to the authentication. The condition is detectable by a test that authenticates as user B and requests a record of user A.

**Root cause.** The role check establishes that the caller is a customer; nothing establishes that the record belongs to that customer.

**Fix.** Scope the query by owner as in `OrderService.get`, or use a bean expression. Prefer non-guessable public identifiers (UUID) as defence in depth, never as the only control. Where records are shared among a team, resolve access through membership instead of a single owner column.

blocks.title: OwnershipTest.java (fragment)

blocks.text: **Prevention.** Include a cross-tenant negative test for every endpoint that takes an identifier; add an anomaly alert on sequential identifier access.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A global `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` also receives `AccessDeniedException` and `AuthorizationDeniedException` thrown from method security, because those exceptions occur inside the controller call. The handler then converts a denial into a 500 or a 200 with an error body, and `ExceptionTranslationFilter` never sees it. Handlers must either exclude these types (declare a narrower handler that rethrows them) or map them deliberately to 403.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is the difference between** `hasRole("ADMIN")` **and** `hasAuthority("ADMIN")`**?** `hasRole` prepends `ROLE_` and therefore matches the authority `ROLE_ADMIN`; `hasAuthority` compares the string exactly. Roles are authorities with a naming convention.
2. **In what order are** `authorizeHttpRequests` **rules evaluated?** In declaration order; the first matching rule decides and later rules are ignored, so specific rules precede general ones and the list should end with `anyRequest().denyAll()` or `authenticated()`.
3. **When does Spring answer 401 and when 403?** 401 when the request has no valid authentication and the entry point is invoked; 403 when an authenticated caller lacks permission. `ExceptionTranslationFilter` decides based on whether the current authentication is anonymous.
4. **How does** `@PreAuthorize` **work internally, and why can it be ignored?** An AOP advisor wraps the bean in a proxy whose interceptor evaluates the SpEL expression through an `AuthorizationManager` before delegating. Self-invocation, private or final methods, objects not managed by Spring and a missing `@EnableMethodSecurity` all bypass it.
5. **What is the difference between** `@PreAuthorize` **and** `@PostAuthorize`**?** The first runs before the method and can use arguments; the second runs after and can use `returnObject`, but the method has already executed and any side effects have occurred.
6. **How is object-level authorisation implemented?** By scoping the query by owner, by a bean-based expression, by `@PostAuthorize` on the result, or by a `PermissionEvaluator`; role checks alone do not prevent IDOR.
7. **How is a role hierarchy configured?** A `RoleHierarchy` bean (`ROLE_ADMIN > ROLE_USER`) for request rules, and the same hierarchy assigned to the `MethodSecurityExpressionHandler` for method security.
8. **Why is** `anyRequest().denyAll()` **recommended?** It converts the rule list into an allow list, so a newly added endpoint is inaccessible until a rule is written for it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Authorisation is a decision over `Authentication` plus a request or method; request rules are ordered and the first match wins, so a final `denyAll()` is the safe default.
- 401 means no valid authentication and 403 means insufficient permission; `ExceptionTranslationFilter` and the chain's entry point decide which one the client sees.
- `hasRole` adds the `ROLE_` prefix and `hasAuthority` does not; token claims must be mapped explicitly to the intended authority names.
- Method security is proxy-based: it is ignored for self-invocation, private or final methods and when `@EnableMethodSecurity` is missing; test the denial.
- Role checks do not protect records; scope queries by owner or use bean expressions to prevent broken object-level authorisation.

Authentication and authorisation control who may call an endpoint. A separate class of attacks abuses the browser, the transport or the shape of the input rather than the identity check: a malicious page causes the browser to send authenticated requests (CSRF), a script reads data across origins, a session identifier is planted before login, an input string changes the meaning of a query, or a flood of requests exhausts the login endpoint. Spring Security provides defences for most of these by default, and several of those defaults are switched off by the most common configuration habit, `csrf.disable()`. This chapter states for each attack the precise condition under which it applies, the Spring mechanism that defends against it, and the configuration that keeps the defence working with a single-page client.

### Concept and mechanism

rows: The browser attaches cookies or cached credentials to a request that a foreign page triggers
`CsrfFilter` with a token the foreign page cannot read; `SameSite` cookies
A foreign script reads a response using the victim's credentials
The attacker sets a known session identifier, the victim authenticates, the identifier becomes privileged
The application is embedded in a hidden frame
Attacker-controlled markup runs in the page
Input is concatenated into a query or command
A request body binds to fields that the client must not set
Credentials or tokens read or altered in transit

blocks.text:
#### CSRF: when it applies and how the token works

Cross-site request forgery exists because browsers attach ambient credentials to requests regardless of the page that initiated them. A page on `evil.example` can submit a form to `bank.example/transfer`; the browser adds the session cookie of `bank.example`, and the server cannot distinguish the forged request from a genuine one. The condition for vulnerability is therefore precise: the application authenticates requests with credentials that the browser sends automatically (session cookies, HTTP Basic or client certificates) and performs state-changing operations on them. An API that authenticates only with an `Authorization: Bearer` header set by JavaScript is not exposed to this attack, because the foreign page cannot make the browser add that header, and there is no ambient credential to abuse. This is the sole legitimate reason to call `csrf.disable()`; the Spring Security reference states the same condition.

`CsrfFilter` implements the synchronizer-token pattern. On each request a `CsrfTokenRepository` provides the expected token (`HttpSessionCsrfTokenRepository`, the default, keeps it in the session; `CookieCsrfTokenRepository` keeps it in the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie). For methods other than GET, HEAD, TRACE and OPTIONS the filter compares the expected value with the value submitted in the `X-CSRF-TOKEN` header (the cookie repository uses `X-XSRF-TOKEN`) or in the `_csrf` form parameter, and calls the `AccessDeniedHandler` with `InvalidCsrfTokenException` (403) on mismatch or absence. Since Spring Security 6 the token is loaded lazily: the session or cookie is touched only when a token is needed. Server-rendered forms obtain the token automatically from Thymeleaf's form support; a single-page application must read it from the cookie and send it in the header.

The default `XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler` masks the token with random data on every rendering to defeat BREACH-style compression attacks, so the value in a rendered page differs from request to request while remaining verifiable. A cookie-based single-page client reads the raw cookie value, which the masked handler cannot accept; the reference documentation therefore provides a `SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler` that uses the masking handler for rendered values and the plain handler for the header (shown in the worked example). Cookies cleared at login and logout require the client to fetch a fresh token before the next unsafe request.

blocks.text:
`SameSite` cookies are a complementary defence: with `SameSite=Lax` (the default of current browsers) a cookie is withheld from cross-site POST requests. It reduces exposure but does not replace the token, because behaviour differs by browser version, `SameSite` relates to sites rather than origins (sibling subdomains remain trusted), and applications may need `SameSite=None` for legitimate cross-site embedding. In Spring Boot the attribute is set with `server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site`.

#### CORS: what it controls

The same-origin policy prevents a script from one origin reading responses from another. Cross-origin resource sharing relaxes it selectively through response headers. CORS is enforced by the browser, not by the server: a request from a non-browser client is unaffected, and a forged request from a foreign page is still *sent* (which is why CORS is not a CSRF defence); only the reading of the response is blocked. Requests that are not "simple" (any method other than GET, HEAD or POST with a simple content type, or any request with an `Authorization` header or JSON content type) are preceded by a **preflight**, an `OPTIONS` request carrying `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`. The browser sends the preflight **without credentials**. The real request follows only if the preflight response carries matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Methods` and `-Headers`.

The security consequence is a classic ordering problem. If the security chain requires authentication for every request, the credential-less preflight is answered with 401, and the browser reports a CORS error even though the CORS configuration is correct. Spring Security solves it with `CorsFilter`, which is placed before the authentication and authorisation filters and answers preflights itself; it is added only when `http.cors(...)` is configured and a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean (or a `CorsFilter` bean) exists. A `@CrossOrigin` annotation or MVC-level `WebMvcConfigurer.addCorsMappings` configuration alone does not help, because the request never reaches Spring MVC.

blocks.text:
Two rules constrain the configuration. `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` cannot be combined with the wildcard origin `*`; the origin must be listed explicitly (or matched with `allowedOriginPatterns`). And reflecting the incoming `Origin` header without validation, which some copy-pasted filters do, is equivalent to disabling the protection.

#### Sessions, headers and transport

**Session fixation.** The attacker obtains a valid session identifier, causes the victim's browser to use it, and waits until the victim logs in. If the identifier is unchanged by authentication, the attacker's copy is now authenticated. Spring Security defends by default with `changeSessionId()` on the Servlet 3.1+ API, which keeps the attributes and issues a new identifier at login; `migrateSession` and `newSession` are alternatives. The related hygiene settings are `HttpOnly` (script cannot read the cookie), `Secure` (HTTPS only) and `SameSite`; in Boot they are `server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only`, `.secure` and `.same-site`. Concurrent-session limits are configured with `sessionConcurrency`.

**Default response headers.** `HeaderWriterFilter` adds `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, max-age=0,` `must-revalidate` with `Pragma` and `Expires`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `X-XSS-Protection: 0` (the legacy browser filter is disabled deliberately) and, only on HTTPS requests, `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 ; includeSubDomains`. The header `Content-Security-Policy` is not sent by default and has to be configured. **XSS and CSP.** Cross-site scripting is prevented first by output encoding at the template layer (Thymeleaf escapes with `th:text`; `th:utext` and string concatenation into HTML do not) and by never reflecting input into script contexts. A Content-Security-Policy limits damage when encoding fails: `default-src 'self'; object-src 'none';` `frame-ancestors 'none'` forbids inline scripts, third-party script origins and framing. JSON APIs additionally return the correct `Content-Type` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. `HttpOnly` prevents a successful script from reading the session cookie; it does not prevent the script from acting as the user.

**Transport.** TLS protects credentials and tokens in transit; HSTS instructs the browser to refuse plain HTTP for the host for the stated period. Behind a reverse proxy or ingress that terminates TLS, the application sees plain HTTP unless the forwarded headers are honoured; without `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` (or `native`) HSTS is not emitted, redirects point to `http://`, and `Secure` cookies may be handled inconsistently.

#### Injection and mass assignment

An injection arises whenever data crosses into a language (SQL, JPQL, LDAP, shell) by string concatenation, so that the data can contain syntax. The defence is to keep code and data in separate channels: bound parameters for values, and an allow-list for identifiers (column names, sort fields) that cannot be bound. The following session against PostgreSQL 16, run on the build machine, executes the SQL that results from concatenation and then the same hostile inputs through a prepared statement, which is the form that JDBC, Hibernate and Spring Data use for bound parameters.

blocks.title: Concatenation versus bound parameters (PostgreSQL 16, run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
Query 2 returns every row; query 3 appends the password hashes to the result set through a `UNION`; the prepared statement treats both inputs as literal user names and returns nothing. In Spring Data, derived queries, `@Query` with `:name` or `?1` parameters, and `JdbcTemplate` with `?` placeholders are safe; string concatenation into `@Query(nativeQuery` `= true)`, `createQuery`, `JdbcTemplate.query` or `Sort` expressions built from request parameters is not.

Mass assignment is the structural counterpart: the framework binds all properties present in the request body to the target object, so a client that adds `"role":"ADMIN"` to a profile update elevates its own privileges if the body is bound to the entity. The defence is to bind requests only to purpose-built DTOs that contain exactly the fields the client may set, and to copy them explicitly.

#### Rate limiting with a token bucket

A token bucket allows a sustained rate with a bounded burst: the bucket holds at most `capacity` tokens, tokens are added at `refill` per second, and each request removes one. An empty bucket means the request is rejected with 429 and a `Retry-After` header. The state per key is two numbers (token count and last refill time), which makes the algorithm cheap enough to run in a filter. The following program runs the algorithm with an injectable clock so that its behaviour is deterministic: a client sending 20 requests per second against a limit of 5 per second with a burst of 10.

blocks.title: Token bucket: 10 burst, 5 per second sustained

blocks.text: The first 13 requests pass (10 from the full bucket plus 3 refilled during the first 650 ms), after which rejections begin with a computed `Retry-After`; over two seconds 19 of 40 requests pass, consistent with the formula in the output. A second client has its own bucket. The key determines the fairness of the limit: the authenticated user name protects against one account being abused, the source address protects unauthenticated endpoints such as login, and a limit by address alone penalises users behind a shared proxy.

blocks.text:
In-process limiters apply per instance: with four replicas a limit of five requests per second becomes up to twenty for the service as a whole. Limits that must be global belong in the gateway or in a shared store such as Redis (see the chapters on gateways and on Redis caching). The in-process filter below is appropriate as a safety net for the login endpoint and for single-instance services.

### Worked example

The web chain below serves a single-page client that authenticates with a server session. It enables CSRF with the cookie repository and the SPA handler from the reference documentation, configures CORS for one origin, hardens headers, limits login attempts per address, and keeps session fixation protection at its default. The API chain from the previous chapters stays separate and stateless.

blocks.title: SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler.java

blocks.text: The rate limiter has two parts. The state lives in a Spring bean so that idle buckets can be evicted on a schedule (an unbounded map keyed by client address is itself a memory-exhaustion vector); the filter is a plain object created inside the security configuration, so that Boot does not register it a second time with the container.

blocks.title: RateLimiter.java
RateLimitFilter.java

blocks.text: `request.getRemoteAddr()` is the address of the direct peer. Behind a trusted proxy it is the proxy address, and every client shares one bucket; with `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` the container resolves the client address from `X-Forwarded-For` for requests from trusted proxies. Trusting that header from the open internet lets an attacker choose a new key with every request, so the trust boundary has to be configured, not assumed.

blocks.code:
@Bean
@Order(2)
SecurityFilterChain webChain(HttpSecurity http, RateLimiter limiter) throws Exception {
    http
        .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())             // uses the CorsConfigurationSource bean
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf
            .csrfTokenRepository(CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse())
            .csrfTokenRequestHandler(new SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler()))
        .addFilterBefore(new RateLimitFilter(limiter), UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
        .sessionManagement(s -> s
            .sessionFixation(f -> f.changeSessionId())         // the default, stated explicitly
            .sessionConcurrency(c -> c.maximumSessions(3)))
        .headers(h -> h
            .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives(
                "default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'"))
            .referrerPolicy(r -> r.policy(ReferrerPolicy.STRICT_ORIGIN_WHEN_CROSS_ORIGIN))
            .httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts
                .includeSubDomains(true).maxAgeInSeconds(31_536_000)))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/", "/login", "/assets/**").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .logout(Customizer.withDefaults());
    return http.build();
}
