blocks.text: The mass-assignment defence is a matter of types. The vulnerable form binds the body to the entity; the safe form binds it to a record and copies two fields.

blocks.title: ProfileController.java

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

The header defaults and the CORS handshake can be checked with `curl`. The output is **typical output (not run on** **the build machine)**.

blocks.code:
$ curl -sI https://app.example.com/api/orders -H 'Authorization: Bearer x'
HTTP/1.1 401
Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: DENY
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 ; includeSubDomains
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer

$ curl -si -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/api/orders \
    -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' \
    -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
    -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type'
HTTP/1.1 200
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization,content-type
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Max-Age: 3600
blocks.title: Response headers and a preflight (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
A CSRF failure is visible both in the response and at DEBUG level, where `CsrfFilter` logs `Invalid CSRF token found` `for http://localhost:8080/api/orders` or, when no session exists, `Could not verify the provided CSRF token` `because your session was not found`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 9: the browser reports a CORS error although CORS is configured

**Scenario.** The frontend at `https://app.example.com` calls `POST https://api.example.com/api/orders` with an `Authorization` header. The browser console reports that the preflight response did not pass the access control check. `@CrossOrigin` is present on the controller and the request works from `curl`.

**Symptoms.** The network panel shows an `OPTIONS` request with status 401 and no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header; the actual POST is never sent.

**Diagnosis.** Reproduce the preflight with `curl -i -X OPTIONS` including the `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method` headers and no credentials. A 401 or 403 means that the security chain rejected it. Confirm with the startup filter list that `CorsFilter` is missing, and in the TRACE log that `AuthorizationFilter` denied an `OPTIONS` request. The third exchange of the preflight diagram shows this sequence.

**Root cause.** The `@CrossOrigin` annotation is processed by Spring MVC, which the request never reaches. The security chain requires authentication for every request, and the preflight is sent without credentials by specification.

**Fix.** Configure CORS in the security chain with a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean and `http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())`, as in the worked example. Do not permit all `OPTIONS` requests globally as a substitute.

**Prevention.** Keep one source of CORS configuration, the security chain; list origins per environment in configuration properties; add a `MockMvc` test that performs an `OPTIONS` request with an `Origin` header and expects the allow headers.

#### Problem 10: POST returns 403 after enabling Spring Security

**Scenario.** A form post or `fetch` call that worked before security was added now fails with 403 on every POST, PUT and DELETE; GET requests are fine.

**Symptoms.** Response status 403 with an empty or generic body; the DEBUG log shows `Invalid CSRF token found` `for ...` or `Could not verify the provided CSRF token because your session was not found`.

**Diagnosis.** Inspect the request: is a token sent in the `X-CSRF-TOKEN` or `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header or in a `_csrf` field? Is the session cookie present (a missing cookie yields the second message)? Is the cookie `XSRF-TOKEN` set in a previous response, and does the client copy it into the header? For a pure token-based API the filter should not be active at all.

**Root cause.** One of three situations: a server-rendered form lacks the hidden token field; a single-page client does not send the token header; or a stateless API chain authenticated by bearer token still has CSRF enabled.

**Fix.** For forms use the template integration that emits `_csrf`. For a single-page client use the cookie repository with `SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler`, read the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie and send it as `X-XSRF-TOKEN`, and fetch the token again after login and logout because the cookie is cleared. For a stateless bearer-token API, disable CSRF **only on that** **chain**, which is justified because no ambient credentials exist. A broad `ignoringRequestMatchers("/api/**")` on a chain that also accepts session cookies is the dangerous variant.

**Prevention.** Document per chain which credential type it accepts and derive the CSRF setting from it; add a test that a session-authenticated POST without a token receives 403.

#### Problem 11: a client elevates its own role through a profile update

**Scenario.** `PUT /api/profile` accepts the `AppUser` entity as body and saves it. A tester sends `{"displayName":"x","role":"ADMIN"}` (or the property that backs the role set) and subsequently has administrator rights.

**Symptoms.** An audit shows role changes without an administrative action; the request log contains unexpected properties in a profile update.

**Diagnosis.** Search the code base for `@RequestBody` parameters whose type is an entity, and for repository `save` calls on a deserialised object. Write a test that posts extra fields and asserts that they are ignored.

**Root cause.** Jackson binds every matching property; the entity contains fields that only the server may change.

**Fix.** Bind to a dedicated record (`ProfileUpdate` in the worked example) and copy the permitted fields. As additional protection, set `spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true` so that unexpected properties are rejected with 400 rather than ignored, and make fields that must never change `updatable = false` in the mapping.

**Prevention.** Rule for reviews: no entity types in controller signatures; separate command and view types. Authorisation-relevant fields change only through dedicated administrative operations that are themselves method-secured.

#### Problem 12: injection through a sort parameter

**Scenario.** A reporting endpoint accepts `?sort=createdAt` and builds a native query: `"SELECT * FROM orders ORDER` `BY " + sort`. Parameter binding cannot be used for column names, so the developer concatenated.

**Symptoms.** Requests such as `sort=(CASE WHEN (SELECT substr(password_hash,1,1) FROM app_user LIMIT 1)='$'` `THEN id ELSE total END)` change the order of results, which leaks data one bit at a time; error messages from PostgreSQL appear in responses.

**Diagnosis.** Search for string concatenation in `@Query(nativeQuery = true)`, `EntityManager.createNativeQuery`, `JdbcTemplate` and `Sort.by` calls whose arguments come from requests. Enable statement logging (`spring.jpa.show-sql=true` or the `org.hibernate.SQL` logger) and look for statements containing request content.

**Root cause.** Identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so the code treated them as trusted text.

**Fix.** Map the request value to a closed set.

blocks.title: SortAllowList.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Prefer derived queries, Specifications and `Pageable` with property validation to hand-written SQL; ban string concatenation into queries in static analysis; run the application database user with the minimum privileges so that an injection cannot read the user table.

### Questions to expect

1. **When is CSRF protection necessary, and when may it be disabled?** It is necessary when authentication relies on credentials that the browser attaches automatically, such as session cookies or Basic authentication. It may be disabled for stateless APIs that authenticate only with a header that scripts set explicitly, such as a bearer token, because a forged cross-site request cannot carry it.
2. **How does Spring Security prevent CSRF?** `CsrfFilter` requires, for unsafe methods, a token that is not available to a foreign page, submitted as a header or form parameter and compared with the value stored in the session or cookie; failures raise `InvalidCsrfTokenException` and produce 403.
3. **Why does a CORS preflight fail on a secured API, and how is it fixed?** The preflight carries no credentials, so an authenticated chain rejects it. `http.cors(...)` with a `CorsConfigurationSource` adds `CorsFilter` ahead of authentication so that it answers the preflight.
4. **Is CORS a security feature of the server?** No. It is enforced by browsers and only controls whether a page may read a cross-origin response; it does not stop requests from being sent and does not protect against non-browser clients.
5. **What is session fixation and how is it prevented?** An attacker fixes the session identifier before login; the defence is issuing a new identifier at authentication, which Spring Security does by default with `changeSessionId()`.
6. **How are SQL injection attacks prevented in a Spring application?** By bound parameters in derived queries, `@Query` with named or positional parameters and `JdbcTemplate` placeholders, by allow-lists for identifiers, and by least-privilege database accounts.
7. **What is mass assignment?** Binding request data to fields the client must not control. The defence is request DTOs with only the permitted fields, optionally combined with failing on unknown properties.
8. **Explain the token bucket algorithm and its advantage over a fixed window.** Tokens refill at a constant rate up to a capacity and each request consumes one, so bursts up to the capacity are allowed while the long-run rate is bounded; fixed windows permit double the limit around a window boundary.
9. **Which headers does Spring Security add by default?** `Cache-Control` (no caching), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and, on HTTPS, `Strict-Transport-Security`; a Content-Security-Policy has to be configured explicitly.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- CSRF applies when credentials are attached automatically; disable it only on stateless bearer-token chains, and use the cookie repository with the SPA handler for session-based single-page clients.
- CORS is a browser rule enforced by response headers; the preflight carries no credentials, so `CorsFilter` must run before authorisation, and wildcard origins cannot be combined with credentials.
- Defaults cover session fixation, framing and content sniffing; a Content-Security-Policy, HSTS behind a proxy and cookie flags need explicit configuration.
- Keep data and code separate: bound parameters for values, allow-lists for identifiers, DTOs for request bodies.
- Rate limit by key with a token bucket; per-instance limits multiply by the replica count, so global limits belong at the gateway or in a shared store.

sections.title: Sessions and Tokens: Choosing an Authentication State Model

blocks.text:
### Model

An authenticated caller must be recognised on every request after the first. Two designs exist. In the **stateful** design the server stores the authentication and the client holds only an opaque reference; in the **stateless** design the client holds a signed statement of the authentication and the server stores nothing. Each choice determines scaling behaviour, revocation, exposure to CSRF and XSS, and the operational dependencies of the service. This chapter compares both with the mechanisms Spring provides, as the basis for the token chapters that follow.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Server sessions

With form login the `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter` stores the `SecurityContext` in the `HttpSession` through `HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository`, and the container returns the session identifier in the `JSESSIONID` cookie. Each later request carries the cookie; `SecurityContextHolderFilter` loads the context from the session into the holder. The session is a server-side map; the identifier is a random 128-bit value that is worthless without the map entry. Logout invalidates the entry and the authentication ends immediately, which is the central advantage of the design. The costs are memory per session, a lookup for every request and a requirement that all instances can reach the session.

With several instances behind a load balancer there are two approaches. **Sticky sessions** pin a client to one instance by cookie or address; they are simple but lose the sessions of an instance that restarts or is scaled in, and distribute load unevenly. **Externalised sessions** store the session in a shared store; Spring Session replaces the container's `HttpSession` implementation with one backed by Redis (or JDBC), transparently to the application code. In Spring Boot the Redis store is configured by adding Spring Session's Redis module (`spring-session-data-redis` with a Redis client; Spring Boot's own documentation names a starter for it in recent versions) and setting `spring.session.timeout`; the auto-configuration replaces the need for `@EnableRedisHttpSession`. Session data is serialised, so session attributes must be serialisable, and the session store becomes a dependency of every request: an outage of Redis becomes an outage of the application unless sessions are allowed to degrade.

blocks.text:
#### Signed tokens

In the stateless design the server signs a set of claims (subject, expiry, authorities) and the client presents the result with each request, normally in the `Authorization` header. Any instance that holds the verification key can validate the token without a store lookup, so horizontal scaling and cross-service calls are straightforward: a downstream service can verify the same token. The price is that a token is valid until it expires, wherever the user logs out; revocation requires extra state (a deny list or short lifetimes with refresh tokens), and claims are visible to the client because a signature provides integrity, not confidentiality.

rows: None for access tokens; refresh tokens need a store
Not before expiry without extra state
No, if sent in a header; yes, if stored in a cookie
Token in script-readable storage is stolen by XSS
Needs the shared store or a gateway
Verifiable by every service with the key

blocks.caption: Sessions and signed tokens compared.

blocks.text:
#### A decision rule

The choice is not "tokens are modern". A same-site web application with one team and a Redis instance already in place is simpler and safer with server sessions and the cookie-based CSRF protection of the previous chapter: logout works, there is no token storage problem in the browser, and permissions can change immediately. Tokens are the better fit when clients are not browsers, when several independently deployed services must verify the caller without calling a central store, or when the identity provider is a separate system (see the chapter on OAuth 2.0). A frequent hybrid is the backend-for-frontend pattern: the browser keeps only a session cookie with a small backend that holds the tokens and calls the APIs, so that no token is ever exposed to browser scripts.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why not store a JWT in `localStorage`, and what is the alternative? Any script that runs in the page, including a script injected by an XSS vulnerability or a compromised dependency, can read `localStorage` and send the token away; the stolen token works until it expires, from anywhere. A token in an `HttpOnly` cookie cannot be read by script but is sent automatically, which reintroduces CSRF and requires the protections of the previous chapter. The robust alternative is a backend-for-frontend that keeps tokens server-side and gives the browser only a session cookie.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Sessions keep state on the server and give immediate revocation at the cost of a shared store; tokens keep state in the client and give local verification at the cost of revocation and storage safety.
- Spring Session moves the session to Redis or JDBC without changing application code; session attributes must be serialisable.
- Cookie-based credentials need CSRF protection; header-based tokens do not, but are exposed to script theft when kept in script-readable storage.
- A backend-for-frontend keeps tokens away from the browser and combines stateless services with cookie sessions at the edge.

A JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519) is a compact, URL-safe representation of a set of claims, usually signed so that a receiver can verify who issued it and that it has not been altered. In a Spring Boot service the JWT replaces the server-side session: the login endpoint issues a token, the client sends it in the `Authorization` header, and every instance verifies it without a shared store. The simplicity of the format hides a large number of ways to use it incorrectly. Most published JWT vulnerabilities are not weaknesses of the cryptography but of verification code that trusts the token to describe how it should be verified. This chapter therefore begins with the byte layout, builds a complete issuer and verifier in plain Java that is attacked for real, and then shows the Spring Security 6 implementation, including refresh-token rotation and logout.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The three parts

A signed JWT (technically a JWS in compact serialisation) consists of three Base64url strings joined by periods. The first is the **header**, a JSON object naming the signature algorithm (`alg`) and optionally the key identifier (`kid`) and type (`typ`). The second is the **payload**, a JSON object of claims. The third is the **signature**, computed over the ASCII bytes of the first two parts joined by a period. Base64url is the URL-safe Base64 variant that replaces `+` and `/` by `-` and `_` and omits the `=` padding, so that a token can appear in a header, a cookie or a URL without escaping.

blocks.text:
The registered claims defined by RFC 7519 that matter for validation are `iss` (issuer), `sub` (subject, the user identifier), `aud` (audience, the intended recipient), `exp` (expiry, seconds since the epoch), `nbf` (not before), `iat` (issued at) and `jti` (a unique token identifier). Application claims such as `roles` are added next to them. Two properties follow from the format. A JWT is not encrypted: placing an e-mail address, a national identifier or a secret in the payload discloses it to anyone who sees the token, including browser extensions and log aggregators; encryption requires the separate JWE format. And a JWT is self-contained: the receiver has no way to learn that the user has since been disabled or has logged out unless it consults additional state.

#### Algorithms and keys

The `alg` header selects one of the algorithms of RFC 7518. Three are in common use.

rows: One shared secret of at least 256 bits
Every verifier can also forge tokens; suitable when issuer and verifier are the same service
RSA key pair, 2048 bits or more
Verifiers need only the public key; the default of the Spring Security resource server
ECDSA key pair on curve P-256
Smaller tokens and faster signing than RSA; JWS uses the raw R and S values, not the DER encoding that `java.security.Signature` returns
blocks.caption: Signature algorithms for JWTs.

blocks.text:
Asymmetric algorithms are preferred as soon as the issuer and the verifier are different services, because a compromised verifier then cannot mint tokens. Public keys are distributed as a **JWK Set** (JWKS) at a well-known URL; each key has a `kid`, and the token header names the key used. Key rotation follows from that: the issuer publishes the new key, begins signing with it, and retires the old key after the longest token lifetime has passed. The Spring resource server caches the JWKS and refetches it when it meets an unknown `kid`.

#### Verification rules

A verifier must decide the algorithm itself and must check every claim that determines whether the token is meant for it. The minimum list is:

1. Parse the token strictly: three parts, valid Base64url, JSON objects.
2. Select the key and the algorithm from **server configuration**, then check that the header `alg` equals it. The header is attacker-controlled input.
3. Verify the signature with a constant-time comparison.
4. Check `exp` (reject expired tokens) and `nbf`, with a small tolerance for clock differences between machines (clock skew). `JwtTimestampValidator` in Spring Security uses 60 seconds by default.
5. Check `iss` against the expected issuer and `aud` against the identifier of this service, so that a token issued for another service of the same issuer is rejected.
6. Check application-level conditions: required scope or role, token type, deny list.

The next program implements issuing and verification for HS256 and RS256 with nothing but the JDK (`javax.crypto.Mac`, `java.security.Signature`, `java.util.Base64`), including two deliberately vulnerable verifier variants that trust the header. It then runs the attacks against both a naive and a strict verifier.

blocks.text:
Reading the output: the first block shows the layout (36 + 130 + 43 characters), the 15-minute lifetime, and the clock-skew behaviour: at 920 s the token is 20 s past its `exp` and still accepted with a 30 s allowance, at 931 s it is rejected. The tampering test changes `role` from `USER` to `ADMIN` without re-signing and fails on the signature. The two attacks succeed against the naive verifier for different reasons.

- `alg` **=** `none`**.** The JWS specification defines an unsecured variant. A verifier that honours `none` accepts any payload with an empty signature part.
- **Algorithm confusion.** A service that expects RS256 verifies with a public key. If the verifier selects the algorithm from the header and passes the same key object to an HMAC routine, an attacker signs a token with HMAC using the *public key bytes* as the secret, which are public by design. The naive verifier computes the same HMAC and accepts it.

Other recurring attack vectors are weak HMAC secrets (next section), `kid` values that the server uses unsafely in a file path or SQL query, header parameters such as `jku` or `x5u` that make the verifier fetch a key from an attacker-controlled URL, and tokens leaked in URLs and logs. Mature libraries such as Nimbus JOSE+JWT, which Spring Security uses, bind the algorithm to the key and reject `none`, but custom verification code does not benefit from that.

#### Access tokens, refresh tokens and revocation

A signed token cannot be recalled, so its lifetime is the revocation delay. The standard design uses two tokens. The **access token** is short-lived (5 to 15 minutes), is sent to the API on every request and is not stored by the server. The **refresh token** is long-lived (days), is sent only to the token endpoint, and is an opaque random value stored (hashed) on the server so that it can be revoked.

Refresh tokens are the highest-value target, because one of them yields new access tokens for weeks. **Rotation** makes each refresh token single-use: every refresh returns a new refresh token and marks the old one as used. All tokens issued from one login share a **family** identifier. If a used token is presented again, either the legitimate client or an attacker holds a copy, and the server cannot tell which; it revokes the entire family, which forces a new login and ends the attacker's access. The following simulation shows the sequence.

blocks.text:
Rotation has a known practical cost: two concurrent refresh calls with the same token (two browser tabs) look like reuse. The refresh endpoint should serialise on the token row, and clients should coordinate refreshes through a single-flight mechanism; some systems add a grace period of a few seconds during which a used token is tolerated.

Access-token revocation (logout, disabled account) needs state or short lifetimes. Three strategies exist. **Short** **lifetimes alone** accept a revocation delay equal to the lifetime. A **deny list** stores the `jti` of revoked tokens until their `exp`, at the cost of one lookup per request and a store shared by all instances (Redis with a TTL equal to the remaining lifetime is the usual choice). A **token version** claim compares a per-user counter in the token with the current counter in the database or cache, which revokes all tokens of a user at once with one lookup.

blocks.text:
#### Where the client keeps tokens

Two places exist in a browser, and both have a cost. Script-readable storage (`localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, a JavaScript variable) is exposed to every script on the page, so an XSS flaw or a compromised third-party script exfiltrates the token. An `HttpOnly` cookie is invisible to scripts but is attached automatically, so it needs CSRF protection and `SameSite`. A widely used compromise keeps the short-lived access token in memory (a JavaScript variable, lost on reload) and the refresh token in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie scoped to the refresh path (`Path=/api/auth`). The page obtains a new access token on load through the refresh endpoint. The stronger design is the backend-for-frontend described in the previous chapter. Mobile clients store refresh tokens in the platform keystore (Keychain, Keystore), not in preferences.

### Worked example

The implementation issues RS256 access tokens, stores hashed refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection, and protects the API with the Spring Security resource server. It builds on the `AppUser` model and the delegating password encoder of the first chapter. Dependencies: `spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server` (which brings `spring-security-oauth2-jose` and Nimbus), `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`, `spring-boot-starter-validation`. The Spring code was not run on the build machine; the signatures were checked against the Spring Security 6.5 reference documentation.

First, the key pair. Keys are generated once, stored outside the repository (a secret store, a mounted volume), and referenced by location.

blocks.code:
$ openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048 -out private.pem
$ openssl rsa -pubout -in private.pem -out public.pem
writing RSA key
$ head -1 private.pem public.pem
==> private.pem <==
-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----

==> public.pem <==
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
blocks.title: Generating an RSA key pair in PKCS#8 and X.509 PEM form (openssl 3.0.13, run on the build machine)

blocks.code:
app:
  jwt:
    issuer: https://api.shop.example.com
    private-key: file:${JWT_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH}
    public-key: file:${JWT_PUBLIC_KEY_PATH}
    access-ttl: 15m
    refresh-ttl: 14d
blocks.title: application.yml (fragment)
JwtProperties.java

blocks.text: The configuration class loads the keys with `RsaKeyConverters` (from `spring-security-core`), builds the encoder for issuing and the decoder for verifying, and combines the default validators (timestamp and issuer) with the deny-list validator. Using `withPublicKey(...).signatureAlgorithm(RS256)` fixes the algorithm on the verifying side; the header `alg` of a presented token cannot change it.

blocks.title: JwtConfig.java

blocks.text: The deny list is a validator. The in-memory map is adequate for one instance; with several instances the same interface is implemented over Redis with `SET jti 1 EX <remaining seconds>`.

blocks.title: TokenDenyList.java

blocks.text: The access-token factory writes the standard claims, a unique `jti`, and the roles without the `ROLE_` prefix; the converter in the security configuration restores the prefix.

blocks.title: TokenService.java

blocks.text: The refresh token is a random 256-bit value. Only its SHA-256 digest is stored, so a database leak does not yield usable tokens (a fast hash is acceptable here because the input is 256 bits of entropy, unlike a password).

blocks.title: RefreshToken.java (accessors omitted)
RefreshTokenRepository.java

blocks.text: The rotation method carries the key subtlety: when reuse is detected it must revoke the family **and commit**, although it then throws an exception. By default a runtime exception rolls the transaction back, which would undo the revocation; `noRollbackFor` prevents it.

blocks.title: RefreshTokenService.java

blocks.text: The controller exposes login, refresh and logout. The refresh token travels only in a cookie restricted to the authentication path; the access token is returned in the body. The `AuthenticationManager` bean is obtained from `AuthenticationConfiguration`, which uses the `JpaUserDetailsService` and the delegating encoder of the first chapter. On refresh the user is loaded again, so that a disabled account or changed roles take effect at the next refresh rather than at the end of the refresh token lifetime.

blocks.title: AuthController.java

blocks.text: Exceptions thrown in the controller layer are translated by an advice. Because `authenticate` throws subclasses of `AuthenticationException` (`BadCredentialsException`, `LockedException`, `DisabledException`), a single handler yields a uniform 401 that does not reveal which condition applied.

blocks.title: AuthExceptionHandler.java

blocks.text: The security configuration for the API chain activates the resource server, maps the `roles` claim to authorities and permits the three public endpoints. The decoder bean from `JwtConfig` is picked up automatically; no property is needed.

blocks.title: JwtSecurityConfig.java

blocks.text:
The refresh endpoint is cookie-authenticated, so a forged cross-site POST to it is conceivable; the cookie attributes `SameSite=Strict` and `Path=/api/auth` prevent the browser from attaching it to cross-site requests. The comment on `csrf.disable()` records the reason for the decision, which a reviewer must be able to check.

For understanding the mechanism, and for the rare case in which the resource server DSL cannot be used, the same behaviour can be written as a filter. The sketch below is educational; production code should use `oauth2ResourceServer`, which also handles error responses, `WWW-Authenticate` headers and DPoP or opaque-token variants.

blocks.title: BearerFilter.java (educational sketch; prefer oauth2ResourceServer)

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

The sequence below exercises login, an API call, refresh with rotation, replay of the old refresh token, and logout. The output is **typical output (not run on the build machine)**; token values are shortened.

blocks.code:
$ curl -si -X POST localhost:8080/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"username":"alice","password":"correct horse battery"}' -c jar.txt
HTTP/1.1 200
Set-Cookie: refresh_token=Qm3x...; Path=/api/auth; Max-Age=1209600; Secure;
    HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict
{"accessToken":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9...","tokenType":"Bearer","expiresIn":900}

$ curl -s localhost:8080/api/orders -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT"
[]

$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/auth/refresh -b jar.txt -c jar.txt
{"accessToken":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9...","tokenType":"Bearer","expiresIn":900}

$ curl -si -X POST localhost:8080/api/auth/refresh -b old_cookie.txt
HTTP/1.1 401
{"status":401,"detail":"authentication failed", ...}

$ curl -si localhost:8080/api/orders -H "Authorization: Bearer $EXPIRED"
HTTP/1.1 401
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token",
    error_description="Jwt expired at 2026-10-19T09:15:00Z"
blocks.title: Login, call, refresh, replay, logout (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The decoded header of the issued token contains `"alg":"RS256"` and the `kid`; the payload contains `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `jti` and `roles`. A quick decode on the command line is `echo "$AT" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d` (the padding may need to be completed, and the result is readable by anyone, which is the point of the earlier remark that a JWT is not encrypted).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 13: a token is accepted after logout or after its expiry

**Scenario.** After the user presses "log out", a copy of the access token still works for several minutes. In a second incident a token created by a custom issuer remains valid for a month although its lifetime should be 15 minutes.

**Symptoms.** API calls with a logged-out token return 200; the audit log shows requests with tokens older than the configured lifetime.

**Diagnosis.** For the first incident the timeline is the one in the logout diagram: the logout handler deleted the refresh token but the access token was verified only by signature and `exp`. For the second, decode the payload and compare `exp - iat` with the expected value: a difference of 900000 instead of 900 reveals that the issuer wrote milliseconds (`System.currentTimeMillis()`) into a claim that is defined in seconds, so the token expires in the year 50000. Also check the server and issuer clocks (`chronyc tracking`, `date -u`) and the configured skew. **Root cause.** Stateless verification cannot know about logout; and a unit mistake in `exp`.

**Fix.** Revoke on logout through the deny list (`TokenDenyList` above) and keep access tokens short; for the unit mistake use `Instant` and the `JwtClaimsSet` builder, which writes seconds, rather than hand-built maps, and add a test that asserts `exp - iat == 900`.

**Prevention.** Document the revocation delay as a property of the design; for high-risk operations (changing a password, transferring money) require re-authentication or a recent `auth_time` claim instead of relying on the access token alone.

#### Problem 14: signing secret hard-coded, weak or leaked

**Scenario.** The HS256 secret is a string literal in `application.properties` (`jwt.secret=secret123`), committed to the repository, and identical in every environment.

**Symptoms.** A security review reproduces a forged administrator token; or, after a repository leak, tokens with arbitrary claims appear in the logs.

**Diagnosis.** Search the repository history for the secret (`git log -S secret123`), and test the strength offline: one token is enough for a dictionary attack. The following run is the attacker's view on the build machine; the throughput varies with hardware, the structure does not.

blocks.title: WeakSecret.java

blocks.code:
$ java WeakSecret.java
dictionary attack: secret = secret123 after 8 guesses
offline HMAC guesses per second on one thread: 433642
8 lowercase letters : 2.09e+11 candidates, 133.8 hours on one thread
256-bit random key  : 1.16e+77 candidates, not searchable
blocks.title: Offline guessing of an HS256 secret from a single token (typical output; throughput varies)

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** HMAC verification is fast, so a short or guessable secret falls in seconds, and a secret in version control is public to everyone with read access, now and in the future history. Because the same secret signs and verifies, any service that holds it can also forge tokens.

**Fix.** Rotate immediately: generate a new key (`openssl rand -base64 32` for HS256, or an RSA or EC key pair), inject it from the environment or a secret store (Kubernetes Secret, Vault, cloud secret manager), never the repository, and invalidate old tokens by changing the `iss`, the `kid` set or the key. Prefer asymmetric keys when more than one service verifies. A start-up check removes the weak-key class of defect.

blocks.title: KeyStrengthCheck.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Secret scanning in CI (a pre-commit hook and a pipeline step), distinct keys per environment, a documented rotation procedure that is exercised, and `kid`-based rotation so that old and new keys overlap.

#### Problem 15: a forged token is accepted (alg = none, algorithm confusion)

**Scenario.** A service uses a small hand-written verifier derived from a blog post, or an old library version that honours the header algorithm. A tester submits a token with `{"alg":"none"}` and role `ADMIN`.

**Symptoms.** Requests with an unsigned or re-signed token succeed; the signature part of the accepted token is empty or was computed with the public key.

**Diagnosis.** Review the verifier: does it read `alg` from the token and branch on it? Does it pass one key variable to several algorithm implementations? Reproduce both attacks as in the plain-Java run above. In Spring, inspect the decoder bean: it must be built with a fixed algorithm (`withPublicKey(...)` with RS256, or `jws-algorithms` in properties), and no custom `JwtDecoder` should parse the header manually.

**Root cause.** The token, which is untrusted input, selected the verification method.

**Fix.** Use `NimbusJwtDecoder` (or the library of the platform) with a fixed algorithm and key, never a hand-written verifier; if a custom one is unavoidable, implement the strict variant shown in the run, which compares the header `alg` with the configured value before any cryptographic operation.

**Prevention.** Upgrade libraries regularly, add a regression test with an `alg=none` token and an HS256 token signed with the public key, and restrict the accepted algorithm list in configuration (`spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jws-algorithms`).

#### Problem 16: a stolen refresh token

**Scenario.** A malware-infected browser extension copied the refresh cookie of a customer. The attacker uses it from another country to mint access tokens.

**Symptoms.** Two clients refresh in alternation; the legitimate user is logged out unexpectedly; logs show refresh calls from different addresses and user agents for one family.

**Diagnosis.** Query the `refresh_token` table by `family_id`: used tokens followed by new ones issued from two different source addresses (store the address and user agent with each token) indicate a fork. The rotation simulation above shows the server-side signature of the event: a presented token that is already marked used. **Root cause.** A long-lived bearer credential without single-use semantics remains valid for whoever holds it.

**Fix.** Rotation with reuse detection (`RefreshTokenService`), revocation of the family, a notification to the user, and binding the token to context where possible (sender-constrained tokens such as DPoP or mTLS in the OAuth ecosystem). Absolute lifetime limits (for example 30 days since login regardless of rotation) cap the damage of an undetected theft.

**Prevention.** Store the token only in an `HttpOnly` cookie or the platform keystore, keep refresh tokens off script-readable storage, alert on reuse events, and provide the user with a list of active sessions with a "sign out everywhere" action that revokes all families of the user.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never log tokens. Access and refresh tokens in request logs, exception messages or analytics events are credentials in plain text for everyone with log access. Mask the `Authorization` header and the refresh cookie in access logs, and in front proxies.

### Questions to expect

1. **What are the parts of a JWT and what does the signature cover?** Header, payload and signature, each Base64url encoded; the signature covers the ASCII bytes of `header.payload` exactly as transmitted. It provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality.
2. **HS256 versus RS256: when is each appropriate?** HS256 uses one shared secret for signing and verifying, so it suits a single service that is both issuer and verifier. RS256 separates the private signing key from the public verification key, which is required when several services or third parties verify tokens; it is the Spring resource server default.
3. **Which checks must a verifier perform?** Signature with a server-fixed algorithm and key, `exp` and `nbf` with limited skew, `iss`, `aud`, and application conditions such as scope, token type and revocation.
4. **What is the** `alg=none` **attack and how is it prevented?** The attacker declares the unsecured algorithm and supplies an empty signature; a verifier that honours the header accepts the token. Prevention is a fixed algorithm in the verifier and the use of a maintained library.
5. **How is a JWT revoked?** Not directly. Short lifetimes bound the exposure; a `jti` deny list or a per-user token version closes the window at the price of a lookup; refresh tokens are stored server-side and revoked there.
6. **Describe refresh token rotation.** Each refresh invalidates the presented token and issues a new one in the same family; presenting an already-used token signals theft and revokes the family.
7. **Where should a browser application store tokens?** Not in `localStorage`. The access token in memory and the refresh token in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie scoped to the refresh path, or a backend-for-frontend that keeps tokens server-side.
8. **How does Spring Security validate a bearer token?** `BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter` extracts the token and calls `JwtAuthenticationProvider`, which uses a `JwtDecoder` (signature and validators) and a `JwtAuthenticationConverter` to build a `JwtAuthenticationToken`; failures go to `BearerTokenAuthenticationEntryPoint` and yield 401.
9. **What is clock skew and what does Spring default to?** The tolerated difference between the clocks of issuer and verifier when checking `exp` and `nbf`; `JwtTimestampValidator` allows 60 seconds by default.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A JWT is signed, not encrypted: integrity and authenticity yes, confidentiality no; the verifier, not the token, must decide the algorithm and key.
- Validate signature, `exp`, `nbf` with limited skew, `iss`, `aud` and application rules; attacks such as `alg=none` and RS256-to-HS256 confusion succeed only against verifiers that obey the header, as the run above demonstrates.
- Short-lived access tokens plus single-use, hashed, server-stored refresh tokens with family revocation give revocation without a lookup on every request; add a `jti` deny list where immediate logout matters.
- In Spring Boot, `oauth2ResourceServer().jwt()` with a `NimbusJwtDecoder` that has a fixed algorithm and a `JwtAuthenticationConverter` for the `roles` claim is the standard implementation; hand-written filters are rarely

justified.

- Keys belong in a secret store, never in the repository; weak HMAC secrets fall to offline guessing in seconds.

JWT login endpoints written by each team solve authentication again and again, and they cannot offer what users and partners expect: single sign-on across applications, login with an existing corporate or social account, and delegated access in which a third-party application acts for a user without ever learning the password. OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) is the standard framework for delegated authorisation, and OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an identity layer on top of it. In a Spring Boot landscape the typical arrangement is a dedicated authorisation server (Keycloak, Spring Authorization Server, a cloud identity provider), web or mobile clients that obtain tokens from it, and Spring Boot services that act as resource servers and only validate tokens. This chapter explains the roles, the grant types, the authorisation code flow with PKCE in detail, the OIDC tokens, and the Spring Security configuration of the three Spring roles: client, resource server and authorisation server.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Roles and tokens

OAuth 2.0 defines four roles. The **resource owner** is the user who owns the data. The **client** is the application that wants access, such as a web application, a single-page application, a mobile app or a backend job. The **authorisation** **server** authenticates the user, obtains consent and issues tokens. The **resource server** is the API that accepts access tokens. The central idea is that the client never handles the user's password: the user authenticates at the authorisation server, and the client receives a token with limited scope and lifetime.

blocks.caption: The user grants consent at the authorisation server, the client exchanges the grant for a token, and the resource server only validates the token it receives.
blocks.alt: 1 grants consent 2 authorisation request, | Client Authorization | Resource owner | web app, SPA, mobile, token request server (IdP) | the user | backend job Keycloak, Spring AS | 3 API call with access token | 4 keys (JWKS) or | introspection | scope = what the client may do | Resource server | aud = which API the token is for | your Spring Boot API | sub = who the user is | The client never sees the password; the resource server never sees the user's credentials.

blocks.text: The **access token** is the credential presented to the resource server. It may be a JWT, which the resource server verifies locally with keys from the JWKS endpoint of the issuer, or an opaque string, which the resource server sends to the introspection endpoint (RFC 7662). Its important claims are `scope` (what the client may do), `aud` (which API it is for), `sub` (the user, or the client in machine flows) and `exp`. The **refresh token** lets the client obtain new access tokens and is handled as in the previous chapter. The **ID token** exists only in OpenID Connect and is a JWT addressed to the client; it states who authenticated and how.

blocks.text:
A frequent error is to use the ID token as an API credential, or to read user attributes from the access token of a third party. OIDC separates the concerns: the client reads the ID token to learn who logged in (validating `iss`, `aud` equal to its own client id, `exp` and the `nonce` it sent) and optionally calls the UserInfo endpoint for more claims; it sends the access token to the API. OIDC providers publish a discovery document at `/.well-known/openid-configuration` that lists the endpoints and the JWKS location, which is what Spring Security uses when `issuer-uri` is configured.

#### Grant types

A grant type is the way in which a client obtains a token. The choice follows from who calls the API.

blocks.text:
- **Authorisation code with PKCE** is the grant for every client that acts for a user, including confidential server-side applications since OAuth 2.1. The client redirects the browser to the authorisation server, receives a short-lived code through the redirect, and exchanges it for tokens over a back channel.
- **Client credentials** has no user: the client authenticates with its own credentials (secret, or a signed assertion, or mTLS) and receives a token whose `sub` is the client. It is the grant for service-to-service calls and scheduled jobs.
- **Refresh token** renews tokens without involving the user.
- **Device code** serves televisions and command-line tools: the device shows a code, and the user approves on a second device.

The **implicit grant** (token returned in the URL fragment) and the **resource owner password credentials grant** (the client collects the password) are removed in the OAuth 2.1 draft and in current security best practice. A client that asks for the user's password defeats the purpose of OAuth, and the implicit grant exposes tokens in browser history and referrer headers.

#### Authorisation code with PKCE

The flow has a front channel (browser redirects, visible to the user and to anything on the device) and a back channel (direct HTTP between client and server). The front channel carries only a short-lived, single-use **code**; the tokens travel on the back channel. The code alone is not enough to obtain tokens, because the token request must also prove that it comes from the party that started the flow.

blocks.text: Four parameters protect the flow. `state` is a random value the client creates, stores and compares when the redirect returns; it binds the response to the session that started the request and defends against CSRF on the callback. `redirect_uri` must match a value registered for the client exactly; this prevents the code from being delivered to an attacker. `nonce` (OIDC) ties the ID token to the request and defends against token replay. **PKCE** (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) defends against interception of the code: the client generates a random `code_verifier`, sends `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA-256(code_verifier))` with the authorisation request (method `S256`), and sends the verifier itself with the token request. The server recomputes the challenge and rejects a mismatch. An attacker who steals only the code, for example through a malicious app registered for the same custom URL scheme, cannot redeem it. The computation can be verified with the test vector of RFC 7636:

blocks.title: Pkce.java

blocks.code:
$ java Pkce.java
RFC 7636 verifier  : dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
computed challenge : E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
RFC 7636 challenge : E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
equal              : true
generated verifier length: 43 characters (allowed 43..128)
token request with the right verifier : code accepted
token request by an interceptor (no verifier): invalid_grant

== refresh token rotation ==
login issued         : rt-...
legitimate refresh   : 200 new refresh to...
attacker replays t1  : 401 REUSE DETECTED -> family fam-1 revoked
legitimate uses t2   : 401 family revoked

blocks.text:
#### The Spring roles

Spring offers a module for each role. **OAuth2 Client** (`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client`) implements the client side: `oauth2Login()` provides login through an OIDC provider (the `OAuth2AuthorizationRequestRedirectFilter` starts the flow, `OAuth2LoginAuthenticationFilter` handles the callback at `{baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}`), stores the tokens in an `OAuth2AuthorizedClient`, and can call APIs with them. **OAuth2 Resource Server** (`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server`) validates bearer tokens, as in the previous chapter, with either a `JwtDecoder` or an opaque-token introspector. **Spring Authorization Server** (the `spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server` module, project version 1.x for Spring Security 6) implements the server role for teams that need their own issuer; for many organisations an existing product such as Keycloak, Okta, Auth0 or Microsoft Entra ID is the more economical choice and Spring Boot services only consume it. A service can combine roles: an API that validates incoming tokens (resource server) and calls another API with a client credentials token (client). A web application with server-side rendering that logs users in with OIDC (client) and then relays the user's token to its APIs does the same. The gateway case, where the token is relayed automatically, is covered in the chapter on securing microservices.

### Worked example

The example secures the order API as a resource server of a Keycloak realm, adds browser login with `oauth2Login`, and shows a service-to-service call with client credentials. The Spring code was not run on the build machine.

**Resource server.** The properties name the issuer; at startup (or on first use) Spring discovers the JWKS URI from the issuer's metadata and caches the keys. The scope claim becomes `SCOPE_` authorities, so scope rules use `hasAuthority`.

blocks.code:
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://sso.example.com/realms/shop
          audiences: shop-api
blocks.title: application.yml (resource server)
ResourceServerConfig.java (fragment of a configuration class)

blocks.text:
With `issuer-uri`, Boot configures a decoder that validates the signature, the timestamps and the `iss` claim; the `audiences` property adds the `aud` check. Keycloak places realm roles in `realm_access.roles` rather than `scope`, so role-based rules need a custom `JwtAuthenticationConverter` that reads that nested claim; the claim structure differs per provider, which is why the converter is application code. Each decision should be taken from the token that the provider actually issues (decode a sample first).

**Browser login.** A server-rendered or backend-for-frontend application logs users in through OIDC. Boot builds the `ClientRegistration` from the properties; the redirect URI default is `{baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}`, and this value must be registered at the provider.

blocks.code:
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          shop:
            client-id: shop-web
            client-secret: ${SHOP_WEB_SECRET}
            scope: openid,profile,email,orders.read
            authorization-grant-type: authorization_code
        provider:
          shop:
            issuer-uri: https://sso.example.com/realms/shop
blocks.title: application.yml (OIDC login)
WebLoginConfig.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
The authenticated principal is an `OidcUser`; a controller reads claims from it with `@AuthenticationPrincipal OidcUser` `user`. Spring Security applies PKCE automatically for public clients (a registration without a secret and with `client-authentication-method: none`); recent versions of Spring Security also apply it to confidential clients, in which case the authorisation request contains `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method=S256`. The exact version in which this default was introduced should be checked against the reference documentation of the version in use.

**Service-to-service with client credentials.** The order service reads stock from an inventory service. It has its own client registration with the `client_credentials` grant, and a `WebClient` that obtains and caches the token and refreshes it before expiry. (The `WebClient` type comes from `spring-boot-starter-webflux`, which may be added next to the servlet stack for this purpose.)

blocks.code:
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          inventory:
            provider: shop
            client-id: order-service
            client-secret: ${ORDER_SERVICE_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
            scope: inventory.read
blocks.title: application.yml (client credentials)
InventoryClientConfig.java

blocks.text:
The service-based manager (`AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager`) works outside an HTTP request, for example in a scheduled job, because it does not need a request-bound repository. The access token is cached in the `OAuth2AuthorizedClientService` (in memory by default) and renewed when it expires, so the token endpoint is not called for every inventory request.

**Spring Authorization Server.** Teams that issue their own tokens add `spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server`, define a `RegisteredClientRepository` with the clients, a `JWKSource` with the signing key, and apply `OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfiguration.applyDefaultSecurity(http)` to a dedicated security chain. The configuration is considerably longer than that of a resource server and requires decisions about key rotation, consent storage and token customisation; it is justified when the organisation needs to own the identity provider, not merely for one application.

### Hands-on

A client credentials token can be requested and decoded from the command line. The output is **typical output (not** **run on the build machine)**; token values are shortened.

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -X POST https://sso.example.com/realms/shop/protocol/openid-connect/token \
    -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=order-service \
    -d client_secret="$ORDER_SERVICE_SECRET" -d scope=inventory.read
{"access_token":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...","expires_in":300,"token_type":"Bearer",
 "scope":"inventory.read"}

$ curl -s https://sso.example.com/realms/shop/.well-known/openid-configuration \
    | head -c 200
{"issuer":"https://sso.example.com/realms/shop","authorization_endpoint":
"https://sso.example.com/realms/shop/protocol/openid-connect/auth",...
blocks.title: Client credentials request against Keycloak (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The decoded payload of the access token for the machine client carries `iss`, `aud`, `sub` (the service-account identifier), `exp`, `scope` and `azp` (the authorised party, the client id). The user flows additionally yield an ID token with `nonce` and `auth_time`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 17: the redirect fails with invalid redirect URI

**Scenario.** Login works on a developer machine and fails after deployment behind a load balancer: the provider shows "Invalid parameter: redirect\_uri" or redirects to a different host.

**Symptoms.** The authorisation server displays an error page before the login form; or the browser reaches the provider with `redirect_uri=http://app.internal:8080/login/oauth2/code/shop`.

**Diagnosis.** Read the `redirect_uri` query parameter of the authorisation request in the browser's address bar and compare it character by character with the values registered for the client at the provider. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy the application builds the URI from the request it sees (plain HTTP and the internal host name), unless forwarded headers are honoured.

**Root cause.** The default template `{baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}` is expanded from the incoming request; the scheme, host or port differs from the registered value, and the provider requires an exact match.

**Fix.** Make the application derive the external URL (`server.forward-headers-strategy=framework`, and a proxy that sets `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host`) or set the redirect URI explicitly in the registration (`redirect-uri:` `https://app.example.com/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}`), and register exactly that value, without wildcards, at the provider.

**Prevention.** One registered redirect URI per environment, tested in the staging environment; never register wildcard redirect URIs, which let an attacker receive the code.

#### Problem 18: valid tokens are rejected with an issuer mismatch

**Scenario.** A resource server in Kubernetes is configured with `issuer-uri: http://keycloak:8080/realms/shop` (the internal service name). Clients obtain tokens through the public URL `https://sso.example.com/realms/shop`.

**Symptoms.** Every call returns 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"` and the log message `The` `iss claim is not valid`; alternatively the service fails to start because the issuer metadata cannot be retrieved.

**Diagnosis.** Decode the token payload and read `iss`; compare it with the configured `issuer-uri` and with the `issuer` field of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` fetched from the URL the service uses. The three must be identical strings. For start-up failures check network reachability and TLS trust from the pod (`kubectl exec` into the pod and run `curl -v` against the issuer URL).

**Root cause.** The `iss` claim contains the URL under which the authorisation server was reached when the token was issued; the validator compares it with the configured issuer literally. Internal and external names produce different strings.

**Fix.** Configure the authorisation server with a fixed frontend URL (for Keycloak, the hostname setting) so that tokens always carry the public issuer, then configure the resource server with that public issuer for validation and, if the public URL is not reachable from the cluster, supply the key location explicitly with `jwk-set-uri` while the issuer check keeps using the public value.

blocks.code:
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://sso.example.com/realms/shop
          jwk-set-uri: http://keycloak:8080/realms/shop/protocol/openid-connect/certs
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Treat the issuer as a contract string; test token validation in an environment with the same topology as production.

#### Problem 19: authenticated but forbidden (scope and audience confusion)

**Scenario.** A single-page client logs in successfully and obtains an access token, yet every API call returns 403. In another case the API accepts a token that was issued for a different API of the same realm.

**Symptoms.** 403 with a valid token (first case); access to data by a client that should not have it (second case).

**Diagnosis.** Decode the access token: compare `scope` (or `scp`) with the authority the endpoint requires (`SCOPE_orders.read` expects the scope `orders.read`), and check `aud`. A token that lacks the scope was requested without it: the client did not include `orders.read` in its authorisation request, or the provider's client configuration does not allow it. A token accepted by the wrong API shows an `aud` that does not name this API, and a resource server without an audience validator.

**Root cause.** Scopes are granted per client and per request; they do not originate in the user's roles. The default `JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter` maps only the scope claim. Audience validation is not performed unless configured.

**Fix.** Request the scope in the client registration and permit it for the client at the provider; configure `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences` or an `OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt>` that requires the expected `aud`.

blocks.title: AudienceValidator.java (fragment)

blocks.text: **Prevention.** Decide per API which scope names exist (`orders.read`, `orders.write`) and which claim carries the audience; include a negative test that a token for another audience is rejected.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Single sign-on with social providers uses the same mechanism: `oauth2Login()` with a registration for Google or GitHub. The identity provider authenticates the person; the application still decides authorisation locally, typically by mapping the verified e-mail or the `sub` claim to a local account and assigning roles itself.

### Questions to expect

1. **What problem does OAuth 2.0 solve?** Delegated access: a client obtains limited, revocable access to a resource on behalf of a user without receiving the user's password.
2. **Distinguish OAuth 2.0 from OpenID Connect.** OAuth 2.0 authorises access to APIs and says nothing about who the user is. OIDC adds an ID token, the UserInfo endpoint and standard claims, and thereby standardises authentication.
3. **Explain the authorisation code flow with PKCE.** The client sends the user to the authorisation server with `state` and a `code_challenge`; after login the server redirects back with a code; the client exchanges the code and the `code_verifier` for tokens on the back channel; the server verifies that the verifier hashes to the challenge.
4. **Why is the implicit grant deprecated?** The access token is returned in the URL fragment, where it is exposed to browser history, extensions and referrers, and there is no client authentication or code binding; the code flow with PKCE replaces it, even for single-page applications.
5. **When is client credentials used?** For machine-to-machine calls in which no user is involved, with the client's own identity as subject.
6. **What is the difference between an ID token and an access token?** The ID token is addressed to the client and proves authentication; the access token is addressed to the resource server and authorises calls. The ID token must not be sent to an API as a credential.
7. **How does a Spring Boot resource server validate a JWT?** It fetches the signing keys from the JWKS URI discovered through the issuer, verifies the signature, checks `exp`, `nbf` and `iss` and optionally `aud`, and maps `scope` to `SCOPE_` authorities.
8. **JWT access tokens versus opaque tokens?** JWTs are verified locally and scale well but cannot be revoked before expiry; opaque tokens require an introspection call per request (cacheable) and allow immediate revocation.
9. **What is the purpose of** `state` **and of** `nonce`**?** `state` binds the callback to the browser session that started the flow (CSRF on the redirect); `nonce` binds the ID token to the request and prevents replay.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- OAuth 2.0 delegates authorisation without sharing passwords; OIDC adds authentication through the ID token; the access token is for the API, the ID token for the client.
- Use authorisation code with PKCE for users and client credentials for services; the implicit and password grants are obsolete.
- `state`, `nonce`, exact `redirect_uri` matching and PKCE each close a specific attack; a computed PKCE challenge can be checked against the RFC 7636 test vector.
- Spring Security provides `oauth2Login`, `oauth2Client` and `oauth2ResourceServer`; a Boot service is usually a resource server of an existing identity provider.
- Issuer string, audience and scope mapping are the three usual causes of valid-looking tokens being rejected or wrongly accepted.

In a monolith the perimeter is the application: one login, one session, one process. In a set of services the same request crosses a gateway and several services, each reachable from inside the network. Security that relies on the network boundary ("internal calls are trusted") fails as soon as one service is compromised or a misrouted request arrives, so each service must establish for itself who is calling and what the caller may do. This chapter covers the identity models for service-to-service calls (user token relay, service identity, mutual TLS, API keys), where validation belongs, and how to test all of it with `spring-security-test`.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Two identities in every internal call

An internal call has two possible subjects. The **end user** on whose behalf the request is made, and the **calling service** that makes it. Authorisation decisions in the callee usually need one or both: "this user may read this order" and "only the order service may reserve stock". Conflating them produces either over-broad access (every service acts as an administrator) or lost audit trails (every action appears to come from a service account). Three mechanisms carry the identities.

- **Token relay.** The gateway or the first service forwards the user's access token to downstream services, which validate it as resource servers. The user identity and scopes arrive unchanged. The token must carry an audience that every receiving service accepts, and a service that relays the token gains the ability to act with the full authority of the user; therefore the audience and scope design must be narrow.
- **Service identity with client credentials.** The calling service obtains its own token (see the previous chapter) and the callee authorises on the service identity and scopes such as `inventory.reserve`. Background jobs and event consumers have no user token and must use this model.
- **Token exchange (RFC 8693).** The service presents the user's token to the authorisation server and receives a new token with a different audience and reduced scope that still identifies the user (and records the acting service in an `act` claim). It combines both identities without handing the original token around; support depends on the identity provider.

blocks.text:
#### Where validation belongs

Validation at the gateway alone is a common design with a standing weakness: any caller that reaches a service directly (a compromised pod, a mistaken route, a developer port-forward) bypasses it. The robust pattern is defence in depth. The gateway validates the token, applies rate limits and rejects obviously invalid requests early, which protects the services from load. Each service additionally runs as a resource server, validates signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and performs ownership checks against the `sub` claim. The cost is one signature verification per hop, which is small compared with the network call. Identity must never be carried in plain headers that a client could set. A header such as `X-User-Id` written by the gateway is trustworthy only if the gateway removes any such header arriving from outside and the services are reachable exclusively through the gateway; the first condition is easy to forget and the second is difficult to guarantee. Signed tokens do not have this weakness.

#### Mutual TLS

Transport Layer Security normally authenticates only the server. In **mutual TLS** (mTLS) the client also presents a certificate during the handshake, so the server knows which service is calling before any application data is exchanged, and the channel is encrypted in both directions. Certificates are issued by an internal certificate authority and are kept short-lived (hours to days) so that revocation is rarely needed. In Kubernetes the usual solution is a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) or a certificate manager that issues and rotates the certificates, leaving the application unchanged. A Spring Boot service can also terminate mTLS itself with `server.ssl.client-auth=need` and a trust store, and read the client identity from the certificate with `http.x509(...)`. mTLS authenticates the service, not the user, so it complements token relay rather than replacing it.
